speechtext:
On June 19 the hon. member for Comox-Alberni asked me several questions referring to overtime and wage rates on federal works at La Scie, Newfoundland. At that time I stated that our Newfoundland officer had been instructed to investigate the complaint and make a report.
The first complaint was that the companies concerned were working their employees in excess of the authorized hours. The second complaint was that they were paying local workers less than mainland workers for the same work; and third, our representative was asked to investigate and determine whether the companies should be required to pay
penalty overtime rates for hours worked in excess of the statutory hours.
Our officer has now reported in the negative on the first two complaints, and on the third that he was making an effort to effect an understanding with the company on the question of overtime payments.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. I note in this morning's press that Vice President Nixon of the United States has issued a warning to the neutral free countries of the world against accepting any economic or military aid from Russia. Does the Prime Minister consider the time has come for a warning from this government to those countries which are being offered Russian aid; that is, a warning as to the dangers of accepting these offers?
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I would hesitate to suggest that the Canadian government issue any warning against the acceptance of aid by less developed countries though, of course, there may be some dangers involved in doing so. But I think the fact that there would be assistance to underdeveloped countries is a meritorious fact in itself. I do not think we would put ourselves in the position where we

Inquiries of the Ministry might appear to be saying you should get the aid and if you refuse to take it from the countries behind the iron curtain we shall see that you get it from other sources. We are not in a position to do that. There has been a lot of propaganda about proffered aid, and I think it has gone beyond the actual benefits that those who seem to have been offered aid would receive from such offers.
It is very difficult to attempt to intervene in the domestic affairs of other countries. Of course a country like the United States may be in a position to say, "If you do not take aid from Russia we shall see that you get it from us", but we are not in a position to make any such broad statement.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned last night at ten o'clock I was trying to show the relation between these Yankee dollars and Canadian jobs. I am not going to keep the house too long today, because I do not want to hold up this session too long; I am very anxious to get back to Vancouver. I am particularly anxious to get back to Vancouver because since I finished the first half of my speech last night and today when I am beginning the second half, I have had news of my second new granddaughter since Easter. I would remind hon. gentlemen of the good old British Columbia custom that whereas fathers must give out cigars when sons or daughters appear, grandfathers always receive cigars from all quarters of the house.
I want to refer particularly to one section of the speech of the Leader of the Opposition when, as reported at page 5780 of Hansard, he said:
We all share the satisfaction in the growth and development that has already taken place. But this is only a promise of what can happen. Government policies should encourage the development of our own resources, should promote the processing of those resources in Canada, should correct our unfavourable trade balance, should assure the participation by Canadians in the development and processing of our resources, and should assure

Natural Resources-Development opportunity and employment for all Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific wherever they may live.
As I listened to the hon. members of the Conservative opposition yesterday developing their case, it seemed to me that I heard echoes of old, unhappy, far-off things and battles of long ago, because there was the distinct echo of 1911 in this approach. I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that there would be now anything as blatant as the slogan which won the election of 1911, namely "No truck nor trade with the Yankees". However, I am submitting that the Conservative opposition are on a slippery slope now, and that they could easily continue down the decline until they got themselves in a position even more dangerous for this country than that of advocating "No truck nor trade with the Yankees" as they did so successfully in 1911.
What I want to show, Mr. Speaker, is that there is a very real connection between these Yankee dollars which some of my hon. friends in the Conservative opposition would keep away from Canada, and Canadian jobs. I do not know whether they would chase out the dollars which are already invested here in the factories, in the pipe lines and in all the other things that go to make up the prosperity of Canada, or whether they would confine themselves to keeping out new investments in Canada; but I want to submit that Yankee dollars invested in Canada mean good jobs for the Canadian people. God help this country if we are ever foolish enough to turn away those Yankee dollars simply to make a convenient election slogan for a desperate party, or for politicians who have not thought things through.
Last night I referred to a very admirable volume, "Canada's International Investment Position, 1926-1954", and I submitted that it is a bargain at $1 from the queen's printer. On page 44 of that volume we get an exact breakdown of all the different industries in Canada, exactly what percentages United States-owned companies obtain in the Canadian market and exactly what percentage of employment is given to Canadians by that United States investment. Working from the bottom upward, 1 shall read the statistics on page 44:

So I should like to know whether there is a single hon. member, even in the Conservative opposition, who will rise in this house and say in all seriousness that he believes the 98 per cent of the jobs which Canadians have in motor vehicle manufacture should be cut off simply because United States investments have provided us with those jobs. So on down the line.
No, Mr. Speaker; when we analyse the Conservative warning about the menace of these Yankee dollars, the menace of this great adverse trade balance about which they -are so fond of talking, we find that adverse trade balance almost entirely made up of tools and capital equipment which is coming in to develop this country. I would ask my Conservative friends to point out the name of the United States-owned factory which they think is a menace to this country. I submit that they are only against this United States investment in general terms, but when it comes down to concrete terms and they are talking about the exact factory or the exact job which is provided by that United States investment they are very vague indeed.
Take my own province of British Columbia. I should like to touch on one or two instances. I will start up the coast at Prince Rupert. I would wager that there is not a single person in the whole city of Prince Rupert who would say that United States investment there has been a menace to that city. As a matter of fact, United States investment in the past few years has transformed the city from one of very moderate progressiveness to one of the most prosperous cities in British Columbia.

I come down the coast to Ocean Falls, where United States investment is entirely responsible for the whole project. I come farther down to Powell River, where there is one of the greatest pulp and paper companies in the whole world. Incidentally, United States investment and for that matter United States management under the Foley brothers, who are among the most enlightened employers in the whole Dominion of Canada, have transformed the city from one which 21 years ago had some of the shadiest labour relations to a city with perhaps the most enlightened labour relations in the whole of Canada. I venture to say there is not even a member of the Conservative opposition who would suggest that is a menace to Canada.
Coming farther down to the city of Vancouver, certainly in my own constituency of Vancouver South I cannot think of any foreign investments that are a menace to Canada. I must say that when I have heard the term "foreigners" used with reference to Americans or "foreign investment" when we mean United States investment I have wanted to cry "shame", because everybody knows that no sensible Canadian ever calls an American a foreigner unless he is deliberately trying to insult him. In any event, in my riding of Vancouver South we welcome foreign investment.
I am sorry to see that my good friend the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is not in his seat at the moment, because yesterday he said he had some sensible things to say about forest production waste and some sensible remarks about what a young Scandinavian had said about our wasteful forest practices in this country. But, Mr. Speaker, never in the history of this young nation, Canada, has there been such an improvement in any industry as there has been in the forest products industry of British Columbia in the past 15 or 20 years with respect to the utilization of materials which formerly went to waste and the better exploitation of the raw materials, especially with regard to the manufacture of plywood.
I would point out that all or most of these improved practices are due to the know-how that came into this country along with some of the refugee capital which came here as a by-product of Hitler's persecutions in Europe. I would say that if there is not a silver lining to every cloud, there was a silver lining at least in one respect so far as Hitler's persecutions were concerned, in that we in British Columbia got fine and enlightened Czech capitalists like the Koerner brothers, who
Natural Resources-Development have not only improved our whole woodworking industry but have made a gift running into millions of dollars for humanitarian purposes in British Columbia.
When I look over the United States-owned factories in my riding and other ridings I invite any member of the opposition to get up and say which American-owned factory he would close down, which American factory he would keep out of the country. There are thousands of people employed in the United States-owned factories, at least a fifth of all the people in Canada. Incidentally, the people with the best jobs in Canadian factories are those who work in these factories created by United States investment.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: What a straw man.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: When I hear the member for Regina City he makes me more homesick than ever, because his voice is exactly like the foghorn in Vancouver harbour. I submit that my hon. friends opposite are in a rather dangerous position. I have no doubt they know full well the meaning of the motion they have moved. It is of course a want of confidence motion, and if it were passed the house would be dissolved and we would have an election now.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: What are you afraid of?

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Of course my hon. friends opposite want an election now, especially the Conservative opposition, because they know very well that unless they get their election before the natural gas pipe line reaches Winnipeg they will be shown up as the most senseless, stupid obstructionists in the whole history of Canada. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, the party that aspires to be the government of Canada and that talks about reducing the adverse trade balance with the United States tries to block the pipe line which is going to substitute Alberta gas for Pennsylvania coal and thereby reduce the largest item that goes to make up this adverse trade balance with the United States.
I know that my hon. friends immediately opposite are in a little different position. They have about four months' extra grace. The poor old Tories there-I must apologize for that term, but it is the result of spending my boyhood days in the city of Hamilton, where people were not only willing to admit they were Tories but were proud of it. I am glad to say that I can remember when the Secretary of State for External Affairs and I lived in Hamilton in our boyhood days. I think he was born into a Conservative family, too. I believe my father was the first

Natural Resources-Development Liberal on our side. We even had an aunt whose name was Aunt Tory; that was her real name, too.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: What party are you going into next?

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
I can think back to my first experience in politics in 1911. I have a horrible admission to make, and that is that even in those days, although my father was a Liberal, the Tories sold me on the idea that if the Liberals won the election we were going to have annexation to the United States. I can remember the great crowds gathering in the dining room of our old home on what was fondly called the mountain in Hamilton, and debating the issue. These debates used to end in real fist fights, which is one reason of course why I felt a little bit at home in this chamber a while ago, because I had been in that kind of atmosphere before long ago.
When I grew up I talked to some of my colleagues like Mr. McGregor and Mr. McTav-ish of the Vancouver Province, who not so many years ago wrote a series of articles about the 1911 election. He gave the inside story of that 1911 election and told how some smart Tory newspaper man from Canada went down to Washington, if you please, and paid those congressman $100 per speech to make speeches in favour of annexation of Canada by the United States. Those fellows would have done it for nothing, especially if they could have had their names across the front page.
May I say that before my hon. friends opposite go farther down the slippery slope of warning against the menace of these Yankee dollars they should keep in mind what happened before. You cannot fool the people twice with the same trick while some of the same people are still alive. Never should they forget that the so-called menace of these United States dollars is the kind of menace which is responsible for one-fifth of the best jobs we have in this country.
I think back to the days of the war when the great Churchill coined one of his most famous phrases when asking for co-operation from the United States. He said, in effect, "Give us the tools and we will finish the job". I submit we could paraphrase that today in regard to this United States investment in Canada which has been responsible for the tremendous development we have had in this country, by saying that they have lent us the tools and we will finish the job; we will carry through from where we are now and proceed with the development of this country. No, Mr. Speaker; the Yankee dollars are not a menace to Canada except in the minds of the hon. gentlemen opposite.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
I do
not intend, Mr. Speaker, to follow my hon. friend in the discussion of the fictional matters in which he indulged. He went back to 1911 and resurrected a fiction that has remained amongst those who do not read and will not hear, that in that election of 1911 this party took the stand "No truck nor trade with the Yankees". This indicates the paucity of argument in regard to the amendment before us, and the extent to which the hon. gentleman felt impelled to go into the fictional past in order to remove himself from the discussion of the present.
But there was one interesting thing I noted in his speech. After he had covered all this historical fiction and myth he finally came to mention the amendment and said, "You want to watch this; if you vote in favour of it we are going to have an election." This indicated that in behind all those words and the creation of all these straw men, there was a fear that could not be hidden. Over and over again-and you, sir, know the circumstances-we on this side of the house have done everything we could to challenge the government to do that thing to which my hon. friend referred a moment ago, but without success.
Now, returning to the amendment, I think at this time it might be well to read that amendment so the discussion might once more return to the subject matter before the house. This is the amendment:
This house is of the opinion that the welfare of the Canadian people requires the adoption now of a national development policy which will develop our natural resources for the maximum benefit of all parts of Canada, encourage more processing of those resources in Canada, correct the present serious unfavourable trade balances, foster wider financial participation by Canadians in the development of our resources, and promote greater opportunity and employment for a steadily increasing population.
I noted, sir, that throughout his remarks my hon. friend dealt with no portion of that amendment. Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition set out in very considerable detail the attitude taken by this party in reference to the need for a development policy that will not only expand and develop Canada today, but preserve and maintain that development for future generations.
The attitude taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was generally to this effect: After all, if we sell our irreplaceable resources in raw form it will be and is to the advantage of the present. The difference between his point of view and that of the Leader of the Opposition is this. The Leader of the Opposition is building for the future; for if we take our irreplaceable resources and move them from Canada in the raw form, the day will

come when, there being none to replace, the advantages of the present will be lost in so far as our national destiny is concerned.
No one has ever taken the stand that it is not to the advantage of this country to have investment from the United States or elsewhere, but what we do say is this. In that investment let Canadian considerations be No. 1, rather than subject to the interests of any corporation from any other part of the world. When you speak of the present and of the need of United States investment in Canada, let me say this. One of the most serious things that has taken place in recent months in connection with Canada's development has been the increase in discount and interest rates, thereby forcing Canadian industry, municipalities and provinces to go into the United States market to borrow because money there is cheaper than it is in Canada.
In today's newspapers parliament learns, as it so often does through the press, that interest rates on bank savings will be increased by one-quarter o.f one per cent after August 1. What kind of encouragement is that to saving in Canada so that Canadians will have money available in order to finance a larger share of Canada's development? Sir, this most niggling, niggardly increase can have no serious influence in causing Canadians to have more money available for investment in Canada. Indeed, the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself, when speaking recently in Hamilton, used these words:
I share the desire of Canadians to be free from dependence on large scale imports of capital. As a member of the Canadian government I do all I can to help maintain conditions favourable for Canadian investors, in the hope that one day we shall be able to look after all our capital requirements if we choose to do so. The plain truth is, however, that Canadians have not generated enough savings to supply all the capital required for Canadian development.
Well, no matter what savings they have generated the government has degenerated them by the heavy rates of taxation that exist, and this latest action of raising interest rates to that extent does not meet the situation and will not meet the situation, nor will it encourage further savings in Canada.
My hon. friend says let us get as much capital into Canada as we can regardless of whether we have any control over it. Well, Mr. James Muir-

Participation by Canadians in enterprises financed by outside (especially American) capital would be greatly encouraged were it not necessary in many cases to buy stock in the parent company in order indirectly to secure some voice in the operations of the Canadian subsidiary. In other words, Canadians should he allowed to buy stock directly in any Canadian corporation.
That point was made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition. Mr. Muir continued:
Another practice, with a similar effect, is that of centralizing research facilities in the non-resident parent company. This practice may result in economies.
Finally, he said this:
I believe that every encouragement and incentive should be given to the establishment, by nonresident corporations, of research facilities in Canada.
I shall deal with that in a moment, for Canadians find themselves in the position where corporations cannot deduct those expenses in Canada to the same extent that they do in the United States, where provision is made to encourage the research so necessary in the developments of today. Yesterday the Minister of Trade and Commerce ridiculed, or endeavoured to ridicule, the arguments advanced by the Leader of the Opposition regarding the fact that development was not reasonably equal in all parts of Canada. The Leader of the Opposition said, as reported at page 5775 of Hansard:
As trustees for future generations of Canadians, we should make sure in every way we can, within the framework of our constitutional structure, that by the combined efforts of all governments and all the people of Canada the opening up of our country brings the maximum benefit to every part of Canada, not only for today but for future generations far into the years ahead.
And then he said this:
Large areas right across Canada have not participated fully in our recent growth and development. This government has failed to meet its obligations to those parts of Canada which are most in need of encouragement and financial support.
To all of this the right hon. gentleman said he had never heard so much rot in one afternoon in his life.

Nor any endeavour on the part of the government to secure it. Last evening the hon. member for Royal dealt with this question, as he has done on previous occasions, and pointed out the injustice and unfairness to the maritime provinces owing to the fact that this government has failed to act, has failed to give any support to the power development on the Saint John river, as it has failed to give assistance to the province of Saskatchewan in connection with the South Saskatchewan dam.
Where are the maritime members now? Today's press records that while the minister was ridiculing the arguments of the Leader of the Opposition, and also in anticipation the arguments raised by the hon. member for Royal, there was a gathering in Fredericton. It was a gathering of premiers, three Liberal and one Conservative. The conference was held. The maritime premiers demand a better deal for the maritimes. They want a coordinated policy, and they went on to point out, "Ottawa helps those who help themselves, but only if they complain loudly enough".
Well, that was the first principle they enunciated. Sir, it is worthy of the attention of the Liberal members from the maritimes, because it should not have been necessary after 20 long years in power for these three Liberal premiers to meet together and determine that in so far as their representation from the maritimes was concerned in government circles, there were insufficient demands for the rights of the people.
Let us go on:
Does the federal government consider that its mission in the development of the Atlantic coast of Canada has been accomplished by sending three geological survey parties to Newfoundland this year, Premier Smallwood demanded?
There is one of the great creative men of Canada. He created the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill). Then we have Mr. Hicks saying:
It is necessary to point out to the federal government that they do not have to think always of Industry in the Montreal-Ottawa-Toronto region, when it comes time to hand out defence contracts. 

Coming back again to Premier Smallwood, speaking as the tribune of the people on behalf of equality of opportunity everywhere in Canada and in particular seeking to equalize those opportunities in the maritimes who said:
"The government of Canada is wrong when they say that all provinces should be treated as equals." The Newfoundland leader borrowed a phrase from communist philosphy to express his attitude: "From each according to his ability, to each according to his need."
The policy of equal treatment, he said, would result in "four, or possibly five, rich provinces, with the rest of us in the poorhouse."
He went on to say there is a faint glimmer of hope:
There is now a glimmering of comprehension in Ottawa, and one of the signs was the appointment of the Gordon commission on the economic development of Canada.
He went on to express the hope that as the result of the work of this commission there may be some action such as the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out over and over again is necessary in this country by way of equalizing opportunities for people in every province of Canada. He goes on to deal with freight rates; he speaks of the unfairness of flat increases that have the result of discriminating against the maritimes and the west, and he concludes by saying that action must be taken in order to secure an equality of opportunity and to raise economic standards in various parts of Canada to the level of other parts of the country. That is the purpose of this amendment. While the Minister of Trade and Commerce was saying yesterday there was no need for this amendment, these men were calling on the government to do the very things which are embodied in the amendment presented to this house.
Sir, it is a very serious question, and one that has been ignored by this government. This government has failed to recognize that every part of Canada deserves its fair share in the national development. It is because of that failure that we in this party have asked among other things that instead of shipping our resources from Canada in their raw form they should be processed here in Canada to the maximum extent.
The hon. member for Vancouver South says there are so many jobs resulting from those raw materials being sent out. I think the number is aproximately 250,000, representing people employed in Canada as a result of the export of raw, semi-raw and partially processed products. There is only a small labour content in raw material. When transferred into processed or semi-processed

material jobs are increased far out of proportion to the extent to which expenditure is necessary to transform those materials into saleable products.
What I want to deal with in particular now in the time at my disposal is one phase of this question that was alluded to by the Leader of the Opposition as part of a development plan. At page 5778 of Hansard he said:
Therefore, the training of skilled men and women to take their part in research and technical development must be part of the national program consciously designed to advance our industrial expansion in Canada.
Without interfering in any way with the exclusive jurisdiction over education which rests with provincial governments, encouragement should be given to advance research and within the framework of our constitution research facilities should be expanded rapidly right across Canada in our universities and industries. This is something the government can do and should undertake right away.
There has been considerable discussion on this subject of the shortage in Canada of trained technical personnel. Gilbert Jackson and associates of Toronto recently summed up their views in anticipation of the situation in Canada in the next ten years and pointed out this fact:
A leading impetus to industrial investment is the prospectively rapid rate of technological advance and automation. The surge in this direction is already under way and tends to feed upon itself. Even the cold war is becoming more and more a race for economic, industrial and technological superiority.
The prospectively rapid rate of technological advance and automation is now seriously threatened by the dearth of engineers and highly trained technicians. This may prove to be the greatest of our handicaps during the next decade.
In other words, training the necessary personnel in Canada under research facilities, either dominion or provincial, or through the instrumentality of business to the end that trained men will be available, is a serious need. Only today there is a report on the university situation in Canada which indicates that during the present year there are some 60,000 students in Canadian universities and eight years from now, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, there will be between 100,000 and 135,000. The U.S.S.R. has not only launched an international trading system but has also launched a vast training system to train the necessary technological workers, scientists, engineers and the like; but while the United States allows almost complete deductions for technical research on the part of industry we in Canada do not do so, nor do we have the opportunity of doing so because United States companies in the main do their research work in the United States. While we in Canada receive an
10, 1956	5821
Natural Resources-Development indirect benefit from that, we do not receive the benefit that we should in keeping Canadians in Canada.
In the last four years the U.S.S.R. has graduated 154,000 engineers; in the same period Canada graduated 6,900 and the United States 116,000. This year the U.S.S.R. will have 60,000 graduates in applied science as compared with 1,700 in Canada, 3,000 in Great Britain and 22,000 in the United States.
Everywhere the fear exists that Russia is outdistancing us and by 1968, according to an estimate that has not been denied, the U.S.S.R. with its present trade policy and its expansive industrial policy will equal the industrial production of the United States. Everywhere the fear is expressed that we are not doing our part nationally or provincially to provide the necessary trained personnel. Within the limits of our constitution, why should not the federal government expand and extend the amount available by way of scholarships in order to encourage and permit universities in this country to take their part in our national development and meet the international challenge presented by the U.S.S.R.?
Sir Winston Churchill warned that the western world is falling behind the U.S.S.R. in advanced training and research in pure and applied science. Last year in Canada one-sixth of the total number of undergraduates were in engineering. The engineering institute of Canada has stated that Russian tactics are building up the world's greatest army of technicians, and this fact should both disturb and inspire us.
I am not suggesting that our institutions of higher learning should become instruments of the state, dominated by the state, but I say this. In order to meet the responsibility of expanding the processing of our commodities in Canada and the development of our industry, we require more and more technicians, far beyond the numbers now being trained. Universities cannot carry on. Fees have increased in several of the universities by from 5 per cent to 11 per cent.
What the Canadian government is doing in these terms is merely touching the outer edge of this responsibility. Last fall they set up a scholarship fund in the national research council which granted some 267 scholarships worth $363,000. Rather, that was the general plan previous to last fall, and there was an increase in that number by 250 summer research scholarships to the value of $200,000. We want to build up in Canada that necessary research army, that scientific corps of trained men. There is no reason why there should be so few scholarships. They do not interfere with provincial rights. That number should be materially increased.

Natural Resources-Development
In addition to that, business should be given encouragement, and companies that come to Canada from outside should be required to provide a certain portion of their earnings for the purpose of research and for the training of research personnel. That is being done in the United States. That has been done in countries in Europe. That today is the purpose of a recent change of front on the part of the U.S.S.R. which, however, goes farther than any of us would wish to go in that it places industrial research and scientific education above any other type of education and denies to a major extent the development of the humanities.
The Globe and Mail of Toronto in March ran a series of articles by Jim Senter in which he set forth in detail the tremendous lack of trained men in Canada, including trained scientists, engineers, electronics technicians and the like. He went on to point out that the army and the air force are short of technical personnel, and that to a lesser degree Canada's defence research board and Atomic Energy of Canada find themselves in a similar situation but not to the same extent as does industry. He also pointed out that in Canada, in the engineering field, in one area to which he made reference approximately one-third of the engineers had come from elsewhere in the world and generally from Europe.
I think one of the main things that can be done today in order to make possible the laying of the foundation for the kind of development the Leader of the Opposition has envisaged as within the capabilities of Canada, would be first to make available the facilities and then train that army of technicians which will be necessary. Then, I repeat, Canadian industries should be encouraged to extend their research facilities by the necessary taxation allowances being provided and companies that come in from the outside, foreign companies, should be required as part of their development to devote a portion of their earnings to the expansion and development of research.
Just one word more, Mr. Speaker. At the beginning I mentioned that the Leader of the Opposition had painted a national picture in which development everywhere would be equalized within natural limitations. I do not want to refer once more to the South Saskatchewan river project, but I say this. Only in the last few days Mr. C. T. Hazen of Saskatoon set out in detail what this great project could achieve in my province. Why does not the government act? It met no opposition from any member of the opposition party. Why should not that project be


a national development? It is one that has received the support of the Leader of the Opposition through the years. It is one that we feel is necessary. It is one more argument in support of those maritime premiers who, meeting yesterday, pointed at the present government of Canada the finger of condemnation for the failure of this government to do that of which the Leader of the Opposition over and over again has stressed the necessity, namely the building up of equal opportunity in all parts of Canada.
Whether it be Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Saskatchewan or British Columbia, the federal authority should be charged with the responsibility of assuring the people living in those areas a reasonable and fair share of the national benefits that for the moment are concentrated to too great an extent in two or three of the Canadian provinces.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment that has been proposed by the Leader of the Opposition raises a number of important points, and in the speeches which have been made by hon. members opposite in support of this resolution a number of these matters have been dealt with.
I think it is quite obvious to all hon. members that in this resolution and in the speeches that have been made by members of the opposition there is nothing that is new. Everything that has been said or suggested has been said before by the same hon. members or by different hon. members in speeches in this house and in speeches outside this house. The wording and intent sometimes differs, but the basic material is the same.
The speeches of the Leader of the Opposition like those of others who have spoken in support of his amendment, were collections of generalities. This has been pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver South a few minutes ago. The hon. member for Vancouver South showed how, when those generalities are reduced to practical examples, the picture that has been painted in the general statement seems to change. I did not see any hon. member across the floor of the house rise to take up his suggestion that they deal with these individual examples that he gave.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that all these generalities are not supported by the facts of our present economic situation in Canada, nor are they supported by the history of the development of the economy of this country over the past 15 or 20 years. Many of these general statements, when taken alone, could perhaps be agreed with. But when they are put together in the form of a more or less connected speech they create an entirely

wrong and incorrect impression, and it is that impression and that wrong implication that requires an answer.
My purpose in entering this debate is only to deal with one or two of the major points that have been raised by several of the speakers opposite. The amendment itself refers to the adoption now of a national development policy which will do certain things. The Minister of Trade and Commerce in his speech in this house last evening pointed out and proved with facts that there is now an existing policy that is being put into effect by this government that it is achieving in very substantial and satisfactory measure the very purposes which are contained in the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition.
This policy is achieving results, as has been proved in a number of fields, and I want to speak of that policy and its results in two important fields. The first is that of research. The Leader of the Opposition mentioned research in a number of places in his speech. As recorded on page 5778 of Hansard of July 9, he spoke of desirable steps to be taken which are necessary to encourage our own management and the expansion of our own affairs. He said this could be done in the important field of industrial research, and he told us of the success achieved in other countries. Then further down the page he went on to speak of university education and research in the universities; and in the next column he spoke of tax deductions that should be permitted to industry in respect of research expenditures, which would encourage our own research in every field.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar also referred to research in his remarks last evening; and the hon. member for Prince Albert, who has just resumed his seat, spoke at some length about the need for research and support of research by the federal government, by provincial governments and in the universities. We have had debates on research in this house in the past, and it is a fact that there has been a very considerable increase in activity and interest in research in Canada over a long period of years.
This increase in activity and interest has accompanied and paralleled the very rapid and satisfactory growth of both our primary and our secondary industries, which was outlined by the Minister of Trade and Commerce last evening. As far as government research is concerned, the federal government is spending this year over $100 million on a wide variety of essential research activities. I am sure it may be said with justice and truth that this represents a per capita expenditure on government research that compares
10, 1956
Natural Resources-Development favourably with similar expenditures in any other country in the world. I think it is also true that the quality of Canadian research and the results achieved fully justify these very large sums of money which have been voted by this parliament and expended by the various agencies and departments of government that exercise responsibility in this field.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the picture will be clearer if I place on Hansard a table prepared from the estimates which summarizes the figures of expenditures on research by the various departments of government. This table indicates that Canadian government research covers a very wide field including the responsibilities of the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, to say nothing of the national research council which is, as hon. members know, the main federal government organization active in the general field of industrial research and pure science. With the permission of the house I shall place this table on Hansard covering the estimated expenditures on research by the federal government for the current fiscal year 1956-57 and for the previous fiscal year 1955-56.

There is, I believe, no question but that the support of the national research council has over the years been a major factor in the development of university research in Canada. I should also point out that the national research council is by no means the only federal government body which is supporting university research. In the year 195455, for example, support for research carried
Natural Resources-Development out in the universities came not only from the national research council but from the Department of Agriculture, the defence research board, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Department of National Health and Welfare, and to a minor extent from other sources. The amounts of these assistances to university research have not been included in the table I have just placed on the record.
The hon. member for Prince Albert laid some stress on the question of industrial research and the steps that should be taken through taxation policy to assist private companies in engaging in industrial research. The Leader of the Opposition took the same line in his speech yesterday afternoon when he said, as found at page 5778 of Hansard:
Tax deductions should be permitted in respect of research expenditures which will encourage our own research in every field.
I find it difficult to understand just how hon. members opposite, in the light of the law as it exists in Canada today, can suggest that this is not being done, in as full a measure as it is done in any other country of the world and in fuller measure than it is done in most countries. The hon. member for Prince Albert said during his speech that we should allow write-offs of research expenditures by industry, and he said we did not do it. That, Mr. Speaker, is just not the law. The law in Canada today with respect to the allowance of research expenditures by private industry is that in so far as current expenditures are concerned expenditures on research are allowed as deductions up to 100 per cent of those expenditures. How anything further could be done than providing a 100 per cent immediate allowance I am unable to imagine.
It is true that the expenditures made must be on a research program approved by the Department of National Revenue, but the regulations and the administration of those regulations are such that any research program even vaguely connected with the industry in which the particular company is engaged or the business that it is carrying on can be an approved project and the expenditures certified for complete write-off in the year of expenditure.
With respect to capital expenditures, which are also a very important consideration in connection with assistance to private firms engaged in industrial research, there is provision for the accelerated write-off of cost of both buildings and equipment, excluding the value of any land involved, over a three-year period. In other words, a company which wishes to do research is permitted to write off its full expense on current account each year 100 per cent, and if the building of any facilities or the provision of any

Natural Resources-Development equipment of a capital nature are required they have accelerated depreciation which permits them to write off those expenses in three years. How hon. members opposite, in the face of that, can suggest that this country is not giving very substantial and effective assistance to companies interested and anxious to go into research projects, I cannot possibly imagine.
The second point with which I should like to deal is one which has been dealt with very briefly by the Leader of the Opposition, in more detail by the hon. member for Royal last evening, and again to some extent by the hon. member for Prince Albert this afternoon. What has been said draws attention to the necessity of the federal authority taking reasonable steps, the best steps that are possible, to assist all portions of this country to develop their economic life on a basis which is fair and equal with the development going on in other parts of the country. Obviously it would be impossible to achieve complete equality of development in a country so diverse as Canada. But it is in this particular field that I think can best be demonstrated the truth of the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce last evening when he said that we have in effect now policies which are doing everything the Leader of the Opposition had in mind in placing his amendment before the house.
The suggestion has been repeated as a generality, but without any attempt to discuss facts or to establish the general statement by facts, that the government is doing nothing to assist the economy of the Atlantic provinces, for instance, in their development in order to try to level out any inequalities there may be there. Let us deal with the Atlantic provinces and the various federal government assistance programs that are being carried out in that area. I say "are being carried out". These are not vague generalities or promises, as are the suggestions made by hon. members opposite. These are actual programs on which money is being spent and through which achievements are being made.
Last night the hon. member for Royal, for example, spoke of the coal industry as one of the basic industries of the maritime provinces, particularly in the province of Nova Scotia. There are federal government assistance programs in effect and being carried out at the present time to assist the coal industry. There are not just one or two programs; they are five in number.
The first one is the transportation subvention on coal movements which is intended to overcome to some extent the handicap of coal mines far removed from the main markets in Ontario and Quebec. This program

was instituted in 1928 and has been in effect ever since. The expenditures under that program are of a substantial magnitude. For example, in the fiscal year of 1954-55 alone the expenditures under this subvention program for mines in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were $8,764,000. Over the period of the whole program from 1929 to 1955 the total amount expended under this program in the two coal producing provinces of the maritimes amounted to $56,066,000.
The second program is the subsidy payments on coal used in the manufacture of iron and steel. This program is designed to place Canadian coal used in the manufacture of iron and steel on a basis of equality with imported coal. These payments have only been made in Nova Scotia, because that is the only Atlantic province in which basic steel is produced. In the fiscal year 1954-55 those payments amounted to $224,000. Since they were instituted in 1931 up to the end of 1955 the total amount paid has been $6,914,000.
The third program provides coal production subsidies, loans and rentals, intended to extend financial assistance with a view to increasing the production of coal in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick mines. This was carried on from 1942 to 1947, the period of this program, with total expenditures amounting to $31,883,000.
The fourth program is coal production assistance, which was instituted to make longterm loans totalling $10 million to operators for the purpose of increasing efficiency of production through expanded and modernized mechanization. This has been in effect since 1949. The total expenditure under that program from 1949 to 1955 in the two maritime provinces has been $8,362,000.
Finally there is an export subsidy program which was brought into effect in 1955 to extend financial assistance in respect of coal from Nova Scotia being shipped outside of Canada during the period June 1, 1955, to March 31, 1956. This program has since been extended. The expenditures under that original program undertaken last year in co-operation with the government of Nova Scotia amounted to $300,000.
Mr. Speaker, that, very briefly, is a description of the actual assistance that has been given by this government to one of the basic industries in the maritime provinces to achieve the very effects of which hon. members opposite are talking. These are not promises. These are not suggestions of what might be done at some future time. Those are actual

programs which hon. members opposite obviously either did not know about or were unwilling to admit in their speeches last night and today.
Let us look a little further than the coal industry. There are two programs of a general nature which are of great value to the maritime provinces. The first is the steamship subvention for coastal services. This is to provide a payment to contractors for service between designated ports in the maritime provinces. This program is not as important as it used to be in some provinces, but over the period 1948 to 1955 the total payments on these steamship service subsidies in the three maritime provinces amounted to $4,644,000. In order to show the importance of this particular program to one of the Atlantic provinces, may I say that these steamship subsidies for Newfoundland in 1954-55 totalled $2 million and the total subsidies paid since 1951 and including 1955 amounted to $8,279,000 for that single province.
Then there is the freight assistance under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. This program is to provide for a reduction of 20 per cent on all rates charged on traffic which originates or terminates in the designated area, which is the maritime area. This was brought into effect under the Maritime Freight Rates Act in 1927. The expenditures for the Atlantic region in the year 1954-55 amounted to $10,590,000, and for the period 1946 to 1955 totalled $77,542,000 for this one program alone. I did not hear the hon. member for Royal mention that program in his speech last night.
The hon. member may be interested in the fishing industry. There are seven programs of assistance supported by the federal government for the fishing industry in the maritime provinces. The first is the fish bounty, most maritime members know about that. It is to aid the development of the sea fisheries of Canada, to encourage the building and fitting of fishing vessels and the improvement of working conditions for the fishermen. In the maritime provinces for the year 1954-55, $120,000 was spent on this program, and from 1946 to 1955 a total of $1,161,000 was spent.
Then there is assistance under the baits service which assists in making supplies of bait available to fishermen. This applies to Newfoundland, and since 1949 the payments made have amounted to $1,019,000.
There is a bounty program for the destruction of harbour seals to protect the fisheries, on which payments have been made since 1946 amounting to $95,000. There is a program of educational services for fishermen
Natural Resources-Development to provide for educational work in cooperative producing and selling amongst fishermen, on which the expenditure has been $459,000 since 1946. There is an annual vote of the Department of Fisheries for industrial development to provide technical services to fishermen and the fishing industry in the maritime provinces. Since 1948 and including 1955 this has cost $658,000, and for Newfoundland from 1953 to 1955, $88,000. Finally there is a program for the construction of bait freezing and storage facilities on which the expenditure in the maritime provinces from 1949 to 1955 has been $101,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that these are important programs of assistance. These are intended to build up the basic industries of the Atlantic provinces, and these are programs that are in effect and achieving results.

Mr. Speaker we have had quite a survey of the industrial development, or lack of development, depending on the point of view, that obtains in Canada. As often happens when I listen to a discussion of this sort I am constrained to wonder if perhaps we do not frequently confuse means and ends. For instance, whenever I pass a particularly large pulp and paper plant in my own constituency, one of the largest in Canada, there is always a question arising in my mind as to just what is the purpose of that particular industrial development. Beyond providing jobs for a certain number of people I must admit I am sometimes in doubt as to whether there is any social purpose at all behind that institution.
I believe when we come to consider the question of the industrial development of Canada we should be asking ourselves not merely how large is that development, not merely how well are we employing our natural resources, but we should also be asking ourselves something else and that is, what is the purpose of our industrial development. As I said, I believe that today we tend to confuse means and ends; we tend to accept as ends industrial development which by the nature of things can only be the means to some real and valuable end.
I do not quite know how one would express that end. Perhaps each individual has his
10, 1956	5829
Natural Resources-Development own definition of it. Possibly the expression "the good life" might be as good a definition as any of the end of social organization and industrial development, for industrial development provides us with the material basis for that good life. I am not for a moment underestimating the extreme importance of that development, but it only provides one of the ingredients of what I think most of us would consider to be the good life.
I would remind hon. members that there have been other systems of society which have had varying degrees of success in industrial development. We have all heard of the success of the late unlamented Adolf Hitler in Germany and we all know, of course, that Mussolini made the trains in Italy run on time. In recent months we have heard a great deal about the industrial success now being achieved in the Soviet union. In each of these instances I have cited there has been brought to the nth degree that confusion of ends and means which I feel afflicts us too in some measure; for while industrial development provides the material basis for the good life for free men and women, it does no more; and as the instances I have cited suggest, if left unchecked by other developments in society it may very well develop into weapons which will more effectively destroy freedom than an underdeveloped economy would be able to do.
Now, to seek the basis for the other aspects of the good life for free men and women we have to look at other institutions and other developments in our society; and I submit, sir, that the basis for the most valuable part of the good life is to be found in the type of social and political institutions under which people live. Here in Canada the fundamental basis of that good life is to be found right in this chamber of the House of Commons, because here in the hands of the 265 members of the Canadian commons rests ultimately complete power over the lives and fortunes of the Canadian people. While it is easy enough for us to take the position that those who now exercise power through the medium of this institution have in their minds and hearts no desire and no intention to infringe on the fundamental rights and freedoms of Canadian citizens, we must also bear in mind the fact that precedents and habits and procedures that are developed in this chamber may at a later stage in our history be used by men with definite intentions to infringe on the freedom, rights and liberties of the Canadian people.
Things have been happening in this chamber of late, sir, that raise some very grave doubts in our minds, doubts as to whether

As I said, there is no doubt that the speech which the minister read was a patchwork of speeches read by the minister elsewhere at different times, and it contains some real highlights. For example, one was his attempt to paint the wonders of Canada's having an adverse balance of trade with the United States. That was something new, I am sure, in the annals of this house; yet the minister tried very hard to make out a case for that point. As reported at page 5796 of Hansard he explained that there was this adverse balance and then he went on to say this:
In fact, for most countries a current deficit of the same relative magnitude as that now being encountered by Canada would mean serious trouble.

But in the following paragraph he has this to say:
In Canada's present circumstances, however, this deficit is not a reflection of weakness but of strength , . .
And a little further on he added this:
I am astonished when I listen to criticism of the current trade deficit, which is so essential to our current phase of expansion and development.
Those remarks, Mr. Speaker, make one wonder whether it is not time that the minister had a new battery of economists advising him. Certainly, if he is right, all the economists in the country are wrong. 1 merely pointed out these statements to show how little value can be placed on many of the statements made by the minister last night.
Then he had another statement to make. It is to be found at page 5801 of Hansard. There he was trying to minimize the extent to which United States capital has been invested in Canada and he pointed out that on a per capita basis Canadians have more money invested in the United States than have Americans in Canada. It sounded like a good plausible argument until one began to read it; and then one could see clearly why it is said that statistics can prove anything. Here we have two countries and there are 15 times as many Americans as there are Canadians. Yet the minister argued that, because the average per capita of Canadian money invested in the United States was greater than the average per capita of United States money invested in Canada, there was therefore no problem. He almost tried to make us believe that Canada was taking over the United States rather than the opposite.
Then in the positive way in which the minister read this speech he once again- as he usually does-tried to make us and the country believe that black is white. But he never quite convinces himself because he always comes in with an addendum, namely that even if black is not white, we ought to consider ourselves lucky that we have black. In that spirit last night he tried to ram quite large quantities of gobbledygook down our throats.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition merited a good deal more substantial consideration than was given to it by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). This amendment sets out one of the long-term policies for Canada of the Conservative party and it was brought forth because we believe in the policy that is to be found in that amendment. I propose to read it again. It is as follows:
This house is of the opinion that the welfare of the Canadian people requires the adoption now 67509-370J
10, 1956	5831
Natural Resources-Development
of a national development policy which will develop our natural resources for the maximum benefit of all parts of Canada, encourage more processing of those resources in Canada, correct the present serious unfavourable trade balances, foster wider financial participation by Canadians in the development of our resources, and promote greater opportunity and employment for a steadily increasing population.
Our objective in that policy would be to make Canada one of the great nations of the world. We believe that is her destiny. We suggest that this policy gives the Canadian people a vision of what this nation can be. We believe that a national development policy -and I stress the word "national" without any apology-if pursued vigorously, would enthuse and inspire Canadians of all ages and would make that vision come true. I suggest to the minister that the Canadian people are not getting much inspiration from any policy or any kind of leadership that has been given by this government in recent months.
In considering this policy I think we should first review Canada's position today-in July, 1956-89 years after confederation. In my opinion here are some of the factors which are of vital importance to a consideration of future Canadian policy. The first is that Canada is still overshadowed by her great and friendly neighbour, the United States. This has been so since confederation and it has been necessary for public men to recognize that fact throughout the whole history of Canada and to adopt policies to counteract it in so far as it was possible to do so. Let us consider confederation itself. One of the main reasons there ever was a Canada was this overshadowing by the United States. Then consider the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That construction took place almost entirely in order that Canada's boundaries might be stretched right out to the-Pacific ocean rather than having the whole northwestern part of the continent become a part of the United States. Today the situation is just the same-namely that we are overshadowed by our great neighbour-and it, probably will be the same for many generations in the future.
Then the second factor, which is vital in my opinion, is that this neighbour is depleting its national resources, and at a much greater rate than the Americans had ever anticipated. In the course of this debate several references have been made to what is known as the Paley report. As the minister knows, that is a report made by what was called the materials policy commission set up by the President of the United States a few years ago. I believe they reported to him in the year 1952.

Natural Resources-Development
I have here an interview with Mr. Paley conducted by the editors of the U. S. News and World Report and contained in the edition of that magazine for August 15, 1952. I propose to read two or three paragraphs because they focus attention on the findings made by Mr. Paley and his fellow commissioners. One answer he gave in this interview was as follows:
A. As a nation we have crossed the great industrial divide. We used to produce more raw materials than we used, but now we are using more than we produce. And this is not a temporary situation. In 1950, we had to import about ten per cent of the raw materials we used, and they cost about 900 million in prewar dollars. We estimate that by 1975 we may have to import about three times as much.
Then he was asked:
Q. Then, the days of ''self-sufficiency'', as you see it, that for generations we have felt that we had, are over?
A. Yes. Our technical people figured that even if we had what we started with-all the materials that were in this country to begin with-it still wouldn't be enough for another 25 years of growing at the rate we've maintained for the last half century.
Another question was this:
Q. What are the principal commodities that are in an unsatisfactory condition today?
A. If you want to get dramatic about it, you could talk about the additive alloys-cobalt, columbium, and such materials as high-grade quartz crystals, mica and industrial diamonds- those materials for which we are largely or completely dependent on foreign supply. But the thing that bothers me most is the lessening adequacy of low-cost supplies of the staples, such as iron, copper, zinc, petroleum, lumber, water for industries, and so forth.
This means that the United States will look more and more to Canada for raw materials in the days that lie ahead, and therefore there will be a more rapid depletion of our own resources than there would otherwise have been. I use minerals as an illustration. There will certainly be a far more rapid depletion of our minerals by reason of this great need which has arisen in the United States. Canada too has a lesson to learn from the Paley report. A few months after it was published, the Bank of Montreal dealt with the question in its monthly Business Review for November 20, 1952, and had this to say:
The commission's policy suggestions and recommendations are, of course, directed to the United States administration. But for Canada the moral is clear. We may reasonably hope to benefit richly over the short and middle term from the colossal appetite for materials of our neighbour to the south;
In my judgment, that is the policy that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is working on. The bank review goes on to say:
__and we may rejoice in our wealth of resources
and our timely capital expansion program. Yet, if the trend is toward an age of scarcity that can
[Mr. Green.l

only be averted by major technological developments, we too may be well advised to do some serious stocktaking for the longer range in the midst of our apparent plenty. For, in the words of the commission, "the consumption of almost all materials is expanding at compound rates and is thus pressing harder and harder against resources which whatever else they may be doing, are not similarly expanding."
Then the third factor in Canada's position today, which is very material, I believe, is this. Our friendly neighbour-and no one questions the wonderful friendliness between the Americans and the Canadians-is unwilling to let Canadian products interfere with the United States home market. I need only mention farm products. Time and again in the past few years we have had moves made by the Americans which have affected our sale to them of farm products, and those moves have been taken on the basis that it was not right to their own countrymen to allow our farm products to take the United States home market. Just last week they made a similar move with regard to a mineral, and I refer to nickel. I have here a dispatch of July 5, just five days ago, from Washington:
The United States is trying to free itself from dependence on Canada for its nickel supplies.
The article goes on to say that already some success is being achieved in reaching that objective.

This desire to become independent of Canadian supplies, these officials say, forms one of the primary aims of a new nickel-purchasing policy announced recently by the office of defence mobilization, the United States government agency charged with stockpiling essential war materials.

Here is a point the government of Canada might note.

speechtext: Fine.

speechtext: Why try to delude ourselves? This has been, is now and will be the basic policy in the United States. As I have said, it is because of that basic policy that they have built such a powerful nation.

The fourth factor which should be considered by Canadians today is this. The Canadian government has been concentrating on trade with the United States. Last year 60 per cent of our exports went to the United States and 73 per cent of our imports came from that country. In this connection we must always remember that we are importing from the United States goods which are far more highly processed than the goods we are sending to them. The very heavy adverse trade balance does not seem to be worrying the minister at all. In fact, he gave us the impression last night that he was very pleased that Canada had such a large adverse trade balance with the United States. To point up the extent of our adverse trade balance I should like to refer to a dispatch I have here of July 6, just four days ago, which has this to say with respect to the importation of consumer goods:
The main rise was from the United States, Canada's top customer and chief source of her imports. Canada's trade deficit with the United States continued to rise to new heights.

-while imports increased by almost $90 million to $404,100,000. . . . For the first five months the Canadian deficit in American trade almost doubled to $625 million from $352,800,000.
The Canadian Statistical Review for June of this year, which we received yesterday, points out on page 4 that the deficit on current account for the first quarter of this year was at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of approximately $1-2 billion. If these adverse balances go on for the rest of the year they will aggregate over $1 billion for the whole twelve months which, as the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) reminds me, will be an all-time record.
The fifth factor which should be considered by Canadians is this. In the last ten years Canada-this has very little to do with any activities by the government-has been discovering raw materials to a far greater extent than at any other time since confederation; oil, natural gas, iron ore, reserves of copper, nickel, uranium, titanium and so on down the list. These discoveries have improved our economy immeasurably. I happened to run across an old advertisement the other day which was published by the government in 1947 when restrictions were placed on trade with the United States. Here is an advertisement headed, "This Is An Emergency-Let's Treat it as Such." The advertisement goes on to say:
Canada is heavily "in the red" in present trading with the U.S. dollar area.
She was not one-half as much in the red as she is now.
In our total trade with the world we are in a good position but not in that part which is done with the U.S. dollar countries.
There is a picture of an oil barrel, a coal scuttle, a bale of cotton and a steel rail, and there are these words:
To keep our industries humming, our living standard high, we need petroleum, coal, cotton, steel and similar essential things.
Our position with regard to at least some of these commodities has greatly improved in the meantime. I realize that the minister said we are still importing as much oil but we are producing a great deal more than we did then. We are to get natural gas and it will be replacing coal to some extent. We have also had the huge discoveries of iron ore. By the way, we should always remember that none of these resources being dug out or pumped out of our soil are inexhaustible. These discoveries have opened wider opportunities for Canadians than we have ever had before, and that very fact alone merits reconsideration of the long-term policy of Canada with regard to future development.

Natural Resources-Development
There are obviously two main roads this country can take in the future. I admit at once that it is largely a matter of emphasis. No matter what government is in power, that government will not be able to follow one narrowly confined policy. It is a matter of emphasis. The first road is to continue concentrating on trade with the United States and to stress the export of raw materials. That is the policy this government is following today. I will not say that they are not doing something about processing materials here. They are, but they are not placing as much emphasis on that type of activity as a Conservative government would do. The Liberal emphasis is on exporting raw materials, and that has been the case right down since the time of confederation, as well as their policy of concentrating on trade with the United States.

I am getting a lot of help here, but unfortunately it is not much good. I should like to read to the minister an extract from a speech made by Dr. Hume with regard to the processing of iron ore in Canada. This speech was made on March 9, 1953. He said:
No one needs to minimize the difficulties of research directed towards the processing of this ore to the pig iron stage at or close to the point of origin.
He was referring to the Quebec-Labrador ore.
But perhaps a really concentrated effort on the part of Canadian metallurgists and scientists would seem important at the present not only to investigate much more fully possible methods of treatment but if present methods are totally unsuited to conditions as we have them, to devise new methods, an accomplishment surely not beyond Canadian inventive capacities.
Then he said:
It is suggested as not beyond the possibilities of our research scientists to find ways and means in
Natural Resources-Development Canada to utilize electric power and iron ore occurring together in the same area to at least effect a partial processing which would be of immense benefit to this country. The Ontario research foundation has been doing excellent work on the study of iron and our mines branch at Ottawa has a number of scientists well versed in the technology of treatment of all kinds of ores. Thus well directed efforts might accomplish much toward reducing our iron ore to the metal before shipment outside Canada . . .
It is not my intention to advocate extreme views in this regard but even a partial solution would bring great additional wealth to this country and show that we are capable of handling our heritage for the welfare of our nation with not only great credit to ourselves but perhaps by discovering new processes we might bestow great benefits on mankind as well.
And then he said:
There is no reason, however, to hesitate to tackle the problem because it is hard and with hundreds of millions of tons of iron ore in sight with mining on a large scale assured for many years a success promises rich rewards nationally.
Then just this year Mr. P. E. Cavanagh, director of metallurgy of the Ontario research foundation, had this to say:
... it appears certain that most of this iron ore will be exported to the United States and Europe.
In this situation it is proper for us to consider means of converting some or all of this Canadian ore into semi-finished or finished products here in Canada. Several proposals for establishing new steel industries in Canada to use large tonnages of this iron ore have already been advanced.
So much for iron ore, Mr. Speaker. Then another example is in the production of heavy water. Canada's whole atomic program is based on the use of heavy water. We are giving a reactor to India and we hope to sell reactors to other nations based on heavy water. For some years there was a plant manufacturing heavy water at Trail. It is true it was owned by the United States but Canadians learned how to manufacture heavy water there. A few months ago that plant was closed and now Canada gets all her heavy water from Savannah, Georgia, the only heavy water plant on this continent. Talk about concentration of nickel and the dangers of concentration-there is the only heavy water plant and this Canadian government has apparently made no attempt whatever to have heavy water produced in this country. We are going to require a great deal of it in the future with new reactors and with the development that takes place, but no move has been made to produce our own heavy water. I might go on to deal with other products, other resources, but my time is running out. I think those will suffice as an illustration of what we have in mind.
Then, the amendment mentions the correction of the present serious unfavourable trade balance. If we process our own resources to a greater degree, that of course would go

Natural Resources-Development some way towards meeting this problem of an adverse balance. I suggest also that we should stop this bowing to Washington at all times. This course has been followed by this government ever since the end of the second war. They hurriedly adopted United States arms for our defence forces to just as great a degree as they possibly could. This attitude has been carried on ever since.
The other day the minister announced the changes that had been made in the GATT agreement. He pointed out that the United States had made concessions to Canada, and that they had benefited and that we had benefited. The Montreal Gazette punched a hole in that argument very neatly when they said that concessions on an equal basis would be all right if our trade were anything like on an equal basis, but it is not. At the same time as there has been this bowing and scraping to Washington, we have had an indifference towards commonwealth preferences. Of course, these preferences were fought tooth and nail by the Liberals in 1932. That party, now in power as the government, had no use for them. The former minister of national defence expressed the attitude of the government very clearly when he was questioned in the house about preferences on October 12, 1949, and the late Tommy Church asked him this question at page 705 of Hansard:
May I say to the hon. gentleman that the proposal also hangs preferential trade on the sour apple tree, like John Brown's body.

Finally, the amendment proposes that wider financial participation by Canadians in the development of Canadian resources should be fostered. Even the members of the government admit that this situation should be remedied, but what do they propose to do about it? So far, we have heard no proposal which would meet that situation. Tax exemptions? No, not a word about that. Tax reductions? Oh, no, they are holding off the reduction in taxation in order to help them win an election next year, although there are surpluses now in the moneys coming into the treasury.
Perhaps this is the most important point of all, because here is a case where a vision could be held out before the Canadian people, a vision of Canada for Canadians. The president of the University of British Columbia summed up the picture very neatly when he spoke in Rochester, New York, about a month ago. President Norman A. M. MacKenzie is not a politician, is not a partisan in any sense of the word. He is one of the outstanding Canadians today. Here is what he told an audience at the University of Rochester:
