speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with considerable interest to the speeches which have been made in the course of this debate. The amendment urges this government to take such steps as will ensure the greater processing of our raw materials in Canada. A great deal has been said in the course of this debate regarding the trade deficit which Canada suffers from at the present time in her trading relations. I think it is only common sense to recognize that any country which is experiencing the industrial development and expansion which Canada is experiencing today requires a great deal of specialized equipment, tooling equipment and other items to expand her industrial potential. I think a striking example of this is the pipe which is being imported into Canada at the present time for the construction of the trans-Canada pipe line which eventually will add a great deal to the industrial development and indeed to production in this country of ours.
In discussing the trade deficit a great deal has been made of the statement that Canada

is suffering an increasing trade deficit as a result of her trading relations. Very little has been said in the course of this debate about the increase in exports which this country is experiencing throughout the world.
In the mail this morning I received the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin for Monday, July 9, and the first paragraph makes interesting reading as far as this debate is concerned. The section is headed: Domestic Exports in May Reached Record Value and Volume
The article states:
Canada's domestic exports reached an all-time high record total for a month of $428,501,000 in May, topping last year's May total of $367,100,000 by 16-7 per cent and bettering the previous monthly peak of $411,700,000 in June, 1953 by slightly more than 4 per cent, dominion bureau of statistics reports in its monthly summary. In the first five months of this year exports to all countries advanced 11-6 per cent to $1,846,300,000 from $1,654,200,000 a year earlier. The volume of exports, also a record, rose 12-5 per cent in May and 7-9 per cent in the 5-month period, while prices averaged 3-8 per cent higher in May and 3-4 per cent in the cumulative period.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these export figures indicate an expansion in our industrial economy which is going forward apace.
On the second page of this bulletin are some rather interesting figures in so far as the group values of exports are concerned. These figures are given in millions, with comparisons for the same period last year. Agricultural and vegetable products, $358 million as compared with $297 million last year; animals and animal products, $102 million as compared with $101 million last year; fibres, textiles and products, $8 million as compared with $7 million last year; wood, wood products and paper, $612 million as compared with $597 million last year; iron and products, $154 million as compared with $128 million last year; nonferrous metals and products, $356 million as compared with $326 million last year; non-metallic minerals and products, $110 million as compared with $71 million last year; chemicals and allied products, $98 million as compared with $92 million last year; miscellaneous products, $44 million as compared with $32 million last year. Across the whole range there has been a substantial increase in our exports in the 5-month period this year as compared with last year.
Then, if we look at the main commodities themselves which are entering into our export trade, I think we can get some idea as to what percentage of those commodities form the raw materials to which the Leader of the Opposition has made reference. At the top of the list we have newsprint paper, a fully processed commodity. We find that in the 67509-371
Natural Resources-Development 5-month period of this year exports of this item have increased from $267 million to $290 million. Wheat, which is incapable of processing, and is generally shipped in its natural state, has increased from $134 million to $191 million. Planks and boards dropped slightly from $151 million to $131 million. Wood pulp, which is capable of further processing, increased from $118 million to $125 million. Nickel increased from $89 million to $93 million. Copper and products increased from $59 million to $85 million. Aluminum and products dropped from $88 million to $80 million. Fish and fishery products rose from $45 million to $46 million. Farm machinery and implements are at the same figure, $42 million.
In this whole range of products which are set out on this sheet, actually the only products which are capable of further processing are wood pulp, nickel in some instances, copper in some instances, zinc in some instances and iron ore. These are our main export commodities, and a very small portion of them is made up of commodities that are capable of further processing in Canada. In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some comparisons between 1939 and 1954.
It is true that in this 15-year period our exports of raw materials increased by 288 per cent but alongside this export of raw materials we find that in this period the index on durable manufactures rose from 107-9 per cent to 297-9 per cent or an increase of 277 per cent, which is less than the increase in our export of raw materials. The index on non-durable manufactures rose from 108-2 to 222-4 or an increase of 206 per cent. I think these figures indicate that where it has been economically feasible secondary industries have been established in Canada at a pace which compares favourably with the increase in our exports of raw material.
If we look at the exports we find that exports of partially and fully manufactured goods have risen in that period from $511 million to $1,846 million or an increase of 361 per cent which is far in excess of the percentage increase of our export of raw materials. Our total export of raw materials in 1954 amounted to $1,082 million. It is interesting to note that of this total figure 75 per cent comprises agricultural and other products which are generally exported in their natural and unprocessed state. The remaining 25 per cent or roughly $304 million were mineral and forest products which are quite capable of further processing.
In the same period in 1954 we imported $473 million worth of raw materials of the

Natural Resources-Development same category and this figure indicates, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce and other speakers have stated, that we are a net importer of raw materials to the tune of roughly $170 million in the year 1954 and not net exporters.
The official opposition in this house has advocated that a policy be adopted by this government of encouraging the maximum processing of raw materials within this country. In the course of the speeches which we have heard I do not think that any definite statement has been made by the Conservative opposition as to how they would achieve this end or just what actually would be done by them, should they form the government, to increase the industrial production in this country. However, I recall that the manufacturers' association of Canada were not quite as wary as the Conservative party concerning what means they would suggest be employed to achieve this end. They stated point-blank that they felt the tariff structure in this country was not such as to encourage the expansion of secondary industries. I believe the figures I have quoted indicate there has been a progressive expansion of industry in Canada and that industries have located themselves in this country where they have found it profitable to do so.
I do not think that in this country there is a lack of businessmen with sufficient foresight that where an industry can be established within the country which can compete with other industries in the home and the world market any opportunity would be overlooked by those businessmen to establish such an industry within Canada.
If the only answer lies in the suggestion of the manufacturers' association, then the work which has been done over the past 25 years in encouraging international trade would be lost. In addition to that we would create in and for Canada a state of economic isolation. We would try to reach absolute self-sufficiency at the cost of isolating ourselves from the trading markets of the world. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if we were to follow that policy we would be going against the record of history. A reading of history indicates to me that in 1930 this method was tried. We tried to isolate ourselves from the other markets of the world and endeavoured to create tariff walls to prevent other people from bringing their goods into this country in competition with our own industrial development. The government of that time no doubt sincerely felt this was the answer, but before its reign was over it found this was
[Mr. Weselak.J
not the answer, and in 1932 the British preferential tariff was brought in in an effort to open the markets of the world to our primary production.
In 1935 the Liberal government came into power and in 1937 a statement of policy was adopted by Mackenzie King in which he stated that this party would bend every effort toward breaking the shackles which prevent free international world trade. I think this government has done that because in the period during which it has been in power protective tariffs in Canada have been reduced by close to 40 per cent and during that period our trade relations with other countries have increased tremendously and our exports have also increased proportionately. By adherence to GATT and bilateral agreements with such countries as Japan and the U.S.S.R. we have opened new markets particularly for our farm products and we expect these markets will be of great benefit to us in the future.
If we were to follow the suggestion of the opposition to its logical conclusion, it would appear to me we would have no alternative but to create an atmosphere wherein we would establish in this country uneconomic secondary industries which would not be capable of competing in the world markets without a certain amount of subsidization or protection. I suggest that the creation of this atmosphere would have an adverse effect upon the economy of this country. If we were to use protection as a means of achieving this end we would soon find we would lose our markets throughout the world.
As has been aptly said, trade is a two-way street. We must buy a certain amount from other countries in order to receive an open port into their markets, and I think this experience is illustrated by the bilateral agreements which have recently been concluded with Russia and which two years ago were concluded with Japan. On the other hand, if we were to try to subsidize these markets we would of necessity have to tax the people in order to meet the cost of such subsidization. If we were to sponsor or force uneconomic industries to establish themselves in this country we would possibly, as I have said, lose our world markets. We would be restricted to our own local markets and as a result we would naturally have to restrict our primary production because we would have no market for it.
This is a serious thing to us in western Canada. Our primary production through agriculture in western Canada is very great. We are dependent for approximately 70 per cent of our production in grain or foreign

markets, particularly in wheat. The expansion of the discovery of raw materials in western Canada has been encouraged by the markets which have been made available for these products and the effect of the development of raw resources in the western provinces is that there have been established service industries and other light industries which are required to service the raw material industry which has been developed as the result of the discovery of such materials, and they are continuing to develop and establish themselves in those particular provinces.
In my own constituency we have a very large pulp and paper mill which is dependent practically completely upon foreign markets. We have recently had brought about mineral developments in the Bird river and Cat lake areas where many metals are being discovered and which are presently being developed and mine shafts being sunk. If we were to adopt the policy of restricting our exports I am sure that these industries would definitely suffer. In my view, this proposition which has been put before the house should be scrutinized very closely. It has many implications which, if carried to their logical conclusion, would certainly have a serious and bad effect upon the economy of the country.

I realize, Mr. Speaker, that this government feels that everything is well as long as they are there. With reckless abandon they disregard parliament, they disregard the opposition, they disregard the people and they say, "All is well so long as we are here". Yesterday evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), I believe, said that we must not be governed by emotionalism and ignorance, that we must view these matters with common sense or in a spirit of common sense and good will. He said he had listened to the greatest rot that he had ever listened to. Then he said, "Do not let us fool ourselves; there are plenty of natural resources; we are not going to be short. There are plenty of them in the world." He said that it does not make much sense to smelt every ton of iron ore and refine every barrel of oil that comes out of the ground.
I could not help thinking of my three or four-year-old grandson setting up a teddy 67509-371J
10, 1958
Natural Resources-Development bear and knocking it down in order to show how strong he was. I could not help thinking how the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was setting up these straw men and knocking them down like a little boy with a teddy bear. We have the minister giving us a lecture about emotionalism and talking nonsense in the house; we have a responsible minister trying to say that to this house. It is bad enough when these Liberal henchmen go out in the country and misrepresent the facts in the country as to what this party stands for. But it is worse to stand here in the house and say that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) implied at any time in his life that every ton of iron ore should be processed in Canada, that every barrel of oil that comes out of the ground should be refined. Mr. Speaker, there is not an hon. member within the sound of my voice nor a child in the Ottawa public schools who does not know better than that.
Mr. Speaker, what we have said in this motion is consistent with Conservative policy all down through the years. It was Conservative policy many years ago-yes, at the beginning of our history of industrial development-that gave birth to industrial development in this country. Even the most bitter free traders of the day, and even a few that may be left yet who still cling to that old dusty halo of free trade, practise the policy laid down by the Conservative party down through the years, namely to raise tariffs instead of lowering them, and other methods, in order to develop industry in Canada. We have no apology to make for that.
I believe, however, that we have common hopes in this house, independent of party, race, class or creed. As Canadians, I believe that we have common hopes in relation to our national security, the defence of our way of life and our survival itself. We have common hopes that we shall become a strong country, that we shall have more people and that we shall have a greater degree of economic independence rather than dependence. I believe those are the common hopes and aspirations of every man, woman and child in Canada who takes time enough to think. The trends, however, are different. No one can study the trends of our development without realizing this. Perhaps the government, in their smug complacency have not bothered to realize that it is nothing they have done, particularly so far as fiscal policies are concerned-for they have not any-* which resulted in the development that has taken place. It is the demand of foreign countries on our resources that are being depleted. It is the demand of $2 billion for expenditures for national defence and other

Natural Resources-Development more or less abnormal features that has kept our prosperity developing as it has lately to a great extent.
There are some things that Canada stands out in. There is no other people with such great resources, as we will all agree. No other country exports more raw resources per capita in world history than Canada has been doing in the last number of years. No other country per capita buys as many of the manufactured goods, the product of other countries' labour, and no other country exports more with less labour. In other words, there is no other country that exports so many dollars worth and that distributes and gives as little benefit to so few people as we do in Canada under our present policy. There is another particular in which Canada stands out. There is no other country in the world that places so many of its trade eggs in one basket. No other country is depending so much on another country. No other country in the free world depends on requirements of other nations so much as does Canada. No other country in the free world needs population more than does Canada and no other country in the free world is increasing its population more slowly.
Why are these things so, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that we have an all-time high national product? Surely that should exercise the dullest mind in this house and even in the country. Why do you boast so much about a great national product of $26 billion and promising to be $28 billion while you are employing on new jobs only half as many as you did in 1952. You say a billion dollars less. Why? Because it takes less men to export our products than it does to finish the product where there is 75 per cent to 80 per cent more finished goods in the last ten years. We need a policy. We need it for our national security. We need it for sound prosperity and economic stability.
In the last ten years, Mr. Speaker, 300,000 Canadians have gone to the United States to find employment in fabricating the raw resources that have gone over there from here. In other words, three have gone to the United States for every one that came to Canada or three times as many. Today, Mr. Speaker, as you well know, as many Canadians from your own native province and from your own great race have down through the years gone to the United States to find employment as you have almost in the whole province of Quebec. Yes, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing that will give employment to more people than will the gradual development of our manufacturing industries. It is important. It will give the maximum benefits to the greatest number of people. It will help


to equalize these benefits among our people. It will help to level out the benefits that we have heard about in this house, where some districts had 30 per cent less benefits in this so-called prosperity in the last few years. It will help to decentralize our development. It will help develop home markets which after all are the best markets. Hon. members speak of what the government has done. Hon. members have talked about the Beechwood development, and they have talked about the Saskatchewan dam. For years they have brought that out at election time but they have never put it into effect yet and they will not do so until after the next election; and if they thought it would not be a tattered and torn issue they would probably save it for the next federal election as they saved reform of the Senate for the last thirty years in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we have an all-time high, it is true, in our national production. But at the same time that is dependent to a great extent on other countries. We are more dependent on our export markets than is any other country. Let us consider the United States and the United Kingdom. As someone has said already today, what has made those countries great? What has made the United States to the south of us the most powerful industrial country in the world?
What made the United Kingdom the great power she has been down through the last century? It was the development of her manufacturing industries, even though she had to import a great deal of her raw resources. Here in Canada we have an abundance of raw resources; and yet we are buying more per capita than any other people in the world of finished manufactured goods and we are exporting more of the raw products. We are dependent on others to market our products. We are dependent on the whims of Washington. We are dependent on the policies of France. We are dependent on the policies of Germany. We are dependent for 17 per cent of our total national output on the whims of others who need our products or who may not need them, whilst the great United Kingdom, with all her problems, is only dependent on four per cent of her national output. We deal almost exclusively with one country; 73-3 per cent of all our purchases last year were from the United States of America, while only 8 [DOT] 5 per cent were from Britain.
We have had a lopsided trade policy down through the years. What has been the result? The government speaks about this party not believing in development. I believe that the Minister of Trade and Commerce tried to imply that it was apparent that we were

opposed to development. There is no party in this country that has a record of national development equal to that of the party I represent here this evening. Down through the years, the national development of our own resources for the benefit of our people has been a fixed policy of the Conservative party, in this country for 75 years. The party to your right, Mr. Speaker, has never been conspicuous for that. They were not conspicuous for that when it was created; they were not conspicuous for that after it was first practised. They opposed it all through the years. They even wanted commercial union with the United States in 1895; in 1911 they wanted reciprocity; in 1930 they wanted countervailing duties; they wanted to go to Washington and find out what Washington thought about fixing tariffs and they would fix them the same. They have no fiscal policy. They have no immigration policy. At the present time they boast about their achievements in the past few years, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce has tried to imply that no other country has made such advancement as we have. No other country has been so dependent on other countries for the requirements of raw resources, which are being depleted. The United States to the south of us needs our raw resources and therefore is buying them from us, it is true; but, so far as the development of manufacturing industries and giving employment to our people are concerned, this government has failed dismally.
No other country in the world has had a greater opportunity to develop manufacturing industries, with the raw resources available here, in the last ten years, than this government has had. Yet we find that we have only a 25-6 per cent improvement in our manufacturing development in the past ten years, while France had a 50 per cent increase, the United Kingdom had a 42 per cent increase, the United States had a 35-5 per cent increase, and communist countries behind the iron curtain have had an increase of over 50 per cent. So on that score we have seen the lack of a policy by this government. We have seen a government tired, smugly complacent, self-satisfied and saying, "Everything is well; we will never run out of our resources." Yet our economists tell us that the visible supply of our chief resources in this country at the current rate of consumption will not last more than 30 years.
Probably the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he says, "That will be enough for us", figures that his government will have pretty well passed by that time. That is not good enough. There is no industry in Canada that could justify its place in the life of this country except by extending
Natural Resources-Development equalizing conditions and extending benefits to the greatest possible number of people. There is no other way. If we are going to be true to ourselves and true to our children's children, we will develop that great heritage of resources in a way that will give the greatest amount of employment to the greatest number of people and equalize conditions through the different parts of this dominion, rather than exporting our resources in the raw form.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce and others have chided the leader of this party about his development policy. Members from the province of Ontario and others who wish to observe it know very well that we have in the province of Ontario many monuments to his policies of development when he was premier of that province. In the district I was very familiar with, I am satisfied there were at least $200 million and at least 30,000 people employed merely because of the development of the resources of northern Ontario set out by the Leader of the Opposition, the Hon. George Drew, when he was premier of Ontario. These things are history. You will find that the history of this country's industrial development has been based more on the sound Conservative policies down through the years than any of the expediencies and shot-gun prescriptions that have been put forth by those who have ridden the gravy train in cold wars and hot wars on these matters and are selling our raw products and our heritage too to people who want them-and risking that they will not want them in the years that lie ahead. Will any hon. gentleman, even those in the back benches who say so little and think so much, they say, pause for a moment and think what will happen if we had anything in the way of a world depression, when these countries would not want some of the raw resources?-We are depending so much more than any-other country on such exports. What would' happen? What would happen if we were not spending $2 billion for defence? It would be most conspicuous then that this government would have no fiscal policy, as they have demonstrated down through the years.
The United States, it is true, has depleted its raw resources, but it depleted its resources as old England depleted hers to a great extent. It depleted them for the benefit of its workmen. The United States is rapidly depleting its resources of iron ore for the great industrial plants of the United States. They are sending their finished products over here at a tremendous rate. In the United Kingdom they do the same thing. The history of these countries and the history of any

Natural Resources-Development country that has had substantial and sound development has been through that development.
This government seems so self-satisfied, even in the face of an increasingly unfavourable trade balance. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said last night, though our trade balance would frighten any other country and in fact would almost ruin many countries, that it was a good thing for this country. That is a strange type of thinking. It is a strange type of logic. It is like telling someone, "Sell a little more of what you have every year and keep buying more, but buy more than you sell and you cannot go broke. It will break another country, but it will not break this country as long as we have a government in power that does not listen to an opposition or is afraid to listen to the people and ignores parliament itself."
This year we are now developing in our trade tendencies the greatest unfavourable trade balance that this country has ever known. In March 1956 we bought $4J million per day more of finished products from the United States than we sold of any of our raw products and all other products combined: $132 million in one month. Yet, even that does not shake the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He says that is a good thing. If that is a good thing, we probably should anticipate a billion and a half, and if it is a good thing probably he and the Minister of Finance will get together and say, "We boasted to the country that we have lowered tariffs at the GATT conference; we will lower some more." If it is a good thing to buy $1J billion more of manufactured goods which our own people could make, it might be a good thing to buy $3| billion more. Then we could be truly the hewers of wood and drawers of water that some of the statements of the government indicate they want us to be. I do not think any of the frontbenchers have actually said that in the house but it has been said outside, and down through the years for the last quarter of a century, yes, for the last half century, many people in Canada have felt that the policies of the party now in power would eventually, if allowed, bring this country to a state of hewers of wood and drawers of water. This is a term that was used in the past but only lately has it been used by their admirers and supporters.
The government seems to think that all is well. They have no manpower policy. They have no fiscal policy, and when they have neither they do not need an immigration policy. They do not have one anyway. We know that immigration into this country is falling down. We will soon be losing more

people than we are gaining. Why, Mr. Speaker, at this late date and in. this dangerous trend we hear these tired old ministers boasting about what they have done in the past, about their past reductions in tariffs at GATT conferences. We see them hiding behind the Gordon commission and dreaming and guessing about the population of Canada in 1980, at the same time not saying why because they are exporting more with less work year by year.
It will take the best ingenuity of industrial leaders and executives and labour leaders and the best ingenuity of a new government to safeguard the sound economic independence and development of this ountry. We cannot boast about our raw resources and the great wealth we are bringing into the country. The United Kingdom has been our best market, but on two occasions we have virtually lost it when the Liberal party was in power. Between 1921 and 1930 we virtually lost the whole British market. We lost it for agricultural products between 1921 and 1930 and we have lost it again to a great extent. Yet down through the years we have had favourable trade balances with that country. Even during the past 10 years we had a favourable trade balance with Britain of $3,413 million and yet in the very same period we bought $7,679 million more from the United States than we sold to that country.
Therefore it is not surprising to find that today the United States owns 91 per cent of our mining and smelting business. It is not surprising that they have a 75 per cent interest in our industrial concerns. It is not surprising that about 50 per cent of all our industrial and primary activities in Canada are controlled by United States investment because we have given it to them in trade balances. On the other hand, despite what the ward politicians out in the country may say, the Conservative party led by the Hon. George Drew has never at any time said that they were opposed to United States investment.

I realize, Mr. Speaker, that under the new standing orders I have only a few minutes to conclude the remarks I was making this afternoon. I wish to summarize what I was saying in connection with our hopes for the development of this country, the employment of our people and the equalization of conditions amongst the various parts of this dominion. I feel that the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) is one which should have been given more serious consideration than it has by this government which has shown distinctly today, and in the last few months, that there is a clear-cut difference of opinion between the government of the day and Her Majesty's loyal opposition. This government has shown all down the years that they believe the development of this country is to be achieved by the exhaustion of our vast resources for the immediate gains that might be brought about through employment of our people. We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition have, since the early days of Sir John A. Macdonald, believed in the development of our own resources for the development of our own people and for the equalization of conditions in the long term interest.
The Leader of the Opposition followed that policy in the days when he was the premier of the province of Ontario, and has emphasized and re-emphasized that the great resources we have, like the great estates of any country or any family, are not inexhaustible. We are the trustees of those resources and we should plan for the future, for future generations. We should try to husband those resources and not to reap the immediate benefits that the members of the government seem prone to emphasize and boast about. As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out yesterday, many of our major resources in this country, great as they are, could be

Natural Resources-Development exhausted at our current rate of consumption within 30 years. Stop and think about it! Some of you men who have children, and who expect their children's children to have opportunities in this country, will realize that these resources should not be exhausted, like the nickel and other resources of this country, in a period of 30 years.
This government has grown very smug and complacent. They have been in power so long, they think nothing matters as long as it does not happen to them. I realize that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is just back from the conference in the United Kingdom. Before he went the Leader of the Opposition urged upon him that he call a conference of the commonwealth prime ministers. The Prime Minister told us on his return that it had been intimated to him that it was not desirable now. He left the impression it may have been intimated by anybody, but it was asked by the Leader of the Opposition and it was refused by the Prime Minister, who took no recommendations over to the conference and brought nothing back. As a matter of fact, he contributed very little to the conference except to tell them how Mr. Eisenhower was going to run his election in the United States. That is not good enough. He told them that about President Eisenhower. If the Leader of the Opposition had said anything like that, he would have been condemned right across the country for interfering in international affairs. The Prime Minister said, "I do not tell you where I stand on anything; I brought nothing in my hands and I take nothing back. I said in the house that I would not do anything without their approval, but I tell you now that President Eisenhower of the United States will make no statement on any great international problem until after the next election." In other words, he interprets Mr. Eisenhower as playing politics, as the Grit politicians in Canada have played it for the last 25 years. Nothing but expediency of the moment: that is the keynote of what you did while you were over there at the prime ministers conference.
I am glad you are back and looking so well.

Mr. Speaker, the grievance I intend to raise is one in which every hon. member of this house is interested because it affects not only my riding but the riding of every hon. member in this house and I would say it possibly affects every Canadian citizen as well, at least those who are interested in what is being done in parliament today. It is not my intention to speak to it at great length because I feel the interest in this subject indicated by certain hon. members of this house is such that every hon. member who cares to do so should be permitted to speak to it.
My grievance is that we as members of parliament do not declare a recess period in summer to afford ourselves an opportunity to visit our constituencies as we should. There are a great many members in this house who are fortunate enough to live within a very short distance of Ottawa and they are able to come here without spending a great deal of time in travelling. I can fully understand that they would feel it is not at all necessary for us to adjourn for the summer recess and go home so that we can visit our constituents. However, Mr. Speaker, may I point out to those hon. members that there is a great deal of difference between the time it takes to travel, let us say from Ottawa to Vancouver or Victoria, or the far-flung parts of the maritimes, and the time involved in travelling from Ottawa to a city like Toronto. For that reason alone, if for no other, I think it is necessary for us to rearrange our business or else find some other means of transportation to enable those members who live a long distance from here to get home to see their constituents.
We in this parliament like to think we conduct the business of the nation in such an excellent fashion that we should receive high praise for it. On the contrary, I would say we mishandle our affairs here by failing to recognize the need for hon. members to go home to see their constituents as well as in the fashion in which we conduct ourselves, which is much worse than most of the Polly pigtail clubs or other literary clubs in the country.
May I point out that to reach the city of Vancouver by train, which is our common mode of travel, it requires at least four nights and three days by ordinary rail traffic-although the Canadian and the supercontinental do it more quickly-and it requires another four nights and three days to

Parliamentarians-Suggested Summer Recess return. In other words we must spend at least a full week in travelling across the continent if we wish to see our constituents. On the other hand it is only a matter of an overnight trip to the city of Saint John, New Brunswick, and those who are fortunate enough to represent a riding in New Brunswick do not find themselves in the same awkward position as do we who come from the far west of our fine country.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that we owe it to our constituents, to our families, to ourselves and to Canada that we have the right to declare a recess here and go home during the summer months when most of our families are on holidays so that at least we may have the privilege of seeing them from time to time. During my short period in this parliament-a matter of three years-we have had three summer sessions. As I stated earlier, I can understand the need, or the lack of need, as is manifest, with respect to the people or the representatives from Ontario and Quebec who live near Ottawa. I can understand that there is no need for a holiday so far as they are concerned. They can go home and examine their constituencies at their pleasure over the weekend or they may meet their constituents over the weekend. As has so frequently been suggested by members in this house, we have our "T to T" boys in the chamber who do not necessarily stay here but who find that their business takes them home and rightfully so. It is much easier to handle the problems of your constituency at home when you have before you the person who has the problem and can discuss it with him at first hand.
I say this. Let us use some common sense. Let us show the intelligence with which we are endowed. Certainly there is no need for us to carry on here year after year during the summer months. We find, for instance, that industry declares a certain holiday for its employees. Management recognize the need for the employees to have a holiday. Management also recognize the fact that they themselves must have a holiday. The holiday might be only for the purpose of visiting their families or their friends. I am not pleading for a holiday, Mr. Speaker. Rather I am pleading for the opportunity for us to get home legitimately, go and see our constituents, talk to them as we should like to do, and hear of their problems at first hand.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) earlier this session asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) to give some consideration to allowing members of parliament from British Columbia and the far west and from the maritimes to have air transportation-that is to have a pass on Trans-Canada


Air Lines-once a session or more often in order to visit their constituencies. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), in the absence of the Minister of Transport, answered the question he was taking it as notice and we have not heard any definite decision on it since. But understandably, I say, as we have heard in the railways, canals and telegraph lines committee room from time to time from the representative of the air lines, Mr. McGregor, this would be a very costly thing as far as Trans-Canada Air Lines is concerned. Seats are at a premium on our air lines. It is a very costly matter. It costs $312.45 to go from here to Vancouver by plane return. To some or to many, possibly, that is not too big a sum and probably they should use their funds for that purpose and spend more time in their constituencies.
Possibly it might be considered that the 21 days we are allowed is sufficient to spend in our constituencies. But, Mr. Speaker, I find-and I am satisfied that many members in this house who have spoken to me on this very same question find the same thing-that the 21 days is in itself not adequate. We must feel free to leave this chamber with the knowledge that the estimates in which we might be interested or some vital piece of legislation that is still before the house or might come before the house might not be brought into the chamber while we are at home and we would not have our constituents tell us that we should have been in the House of Commons to speak to that particular question.
The opportunity for members of parliament to take part in the normal civic affairs on Dominion day and other holidays during that season is lost because we find that it is necessary for us from the far west to stay in this chamber to take part in the discussions or to look after our business from this point of view. After all, that is the reason we are being paid; or one of the reasons we are being paid is to be doing our business in Ottawa. It is true that we might go home and say, "We are home on parliamentary business". I would admit that. But, Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, it takes us four nights and three days by train to reach Vancouver and another four nights and three days to come back; in other words if we are to spend a week in our constituencies, it would take three weeks for a British Columbia member to do his job at home and use the train going and coming. Mr. Speaker, I feel that that is a mistake. We should declare a recess just the same as would any other common-sense business enterprise, and get our business done. I am satisfied that if that were done and if we, let us say, declared our recess some time before July 1 and had

only one month recess or two months, as the case might be, whatever is decided upon, we would get a great deal more business done before June 30 than we are getting done at the present time. I think that a great deal of our time is being spent in not doing the business that we have been sent down here to do because so many of us,- and not for political reasons-by reason of the fact that they cannot see their constituents, are frustrated from time to time by knowing full well that certain of the estimates or other business will be before the house when they are at home trying to look after their constituencies.
We recognize, Mr. Speaker, that there is need for a recess period at Easter so that members of parliament can go home to see their constituents at that time. How much truer it is to recognize the fact that it is more important to go home during the early part of July or all of July and part of August and carry on later in the year again and finish the legislation in a common-sense fashion. Mr. Speaker, it may be that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the government may feel that it is impossible for us to finish our business in ten months' time. I have been given to understand heretofore that the government has felt that we should finish our business by June. This suggested procedure would at least give them the opportunity of trying to get it done by that time. Certain individuals may argue that it might be impractical, that we might reach the stage, let us say, toward the end of June when it became apparent that an extra week of sitting would finish our legislation and we would be finished for the year. To them 1 would say that certainly we should be able to revise the rules in order to make it possible for us, by unanimous consent, to decide to continue to sit for that extra week, as the case might be, and finish the business for the year. But, Mr. Speaker, I feel-and I am satisfied that there are many more in this house who feel likewise-that we should have a recess during which we can visit our constituents and for which we can plan so that we can tell our constituents we will be home during that particular time of the year. I find that the constituents-many of them in my riding at least, and I am satisfied that the same applies to many other ridings- do not realize that their legislators do not regulate their business so that they can be home for events such as Dominion day and on other occasions, as they might expect them to be.
I would say that we should change our rules to call for a recess possibly of one month-it might be found convenient to have a two-month recess-not for holidays but to
Parliamentarians-Suggested Summer Recess go home so that we can look after the business properly as we are expected to do in our own ridings, at least during the summer months.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to state a grievance. In doing so, I speak on behalf of this group and I believe I speak on behalf of the institution of parliament and on behalf of the good name of this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
My grievance is against the Prime Minister. I do not propose to rehash any of the events which are part of the records of this session of this parliament prior to a few days ago; but I feel that in addition to the injury that has been done to parliament in this session a further insult was added yesterday by the Prime Minister.
There are certain matters which are the prerogative of the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker. Those matters include a number of important considerations, one of them being

the decision as to who will preside over the deliberations of this house. This is provided for, Mr. Speaker, not in anything that is temporary or passing but in the British North America Act itself. Section 44 of the British North America Act reads as follows:
The House of Commons on its first assembling after a general election shall proceed with all practicable speed to elect one of its members to be Speaker.
Section 45 reads:
In case of a vacancy happening in the office of Speaker by death, resignation, or otherwise, the House of Commons shall with all practicable speed proceed to elect another of its members to be Speaker.
Surely, I do not need to emphasize the point that it is laid down clearly in the constitution of this country that it is the House of Commons, not the government, not the Prime Minister, but the House of Commons that decides who shall be its Speaker. In this connection, there is an interesting citation in Beauchesne's third edition, citation 35, which reads as follows:
The choice of Speaker is the choice of this house. The house chooses and elects its Speaker; he is in no sense the choice of the government-in no sense the choice of the Prime Minister. In the British house, this has been the practice since the earliest times; we have followed that custom in equal degree and with equal fidelity. Indeed, in the British parliament it has never been the practice even for a member of the government to move or second the selection of a Speaker; that is left to the private members.
I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that that is a quotation from a speech made in this house by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. I think it is properly included in Beauchesne's third edition as an annotation to the sections of the British North America Act that I read a moment ago.
Perhaps I might read as well a few lines from the next citation in Beauchesne's third edition, citation 36:
Mr. Pitt once intended to propose Mr. Addington, but Mr. Hatsell, Clerk of the house, on being consulted by Mr. Addington, said; "I think that the choice of the speaker should not be on the motion of the minister. Indeed an invidious use might be made of it, to represent you as the friend of the minister, rather than the choice of the house." Mr. Pitt acknowledged the force of this objection.
Mr. Speaker, I am ready to admit that it took quite a few years for the Canadian House of Commons to develop a tradition with regard to the choice of its speaker. I read again today the account of the sitting of the House of Commons the first day it met in 1867 and there was a dispute on that very first day over the choice of the speaker proposed on that occasion by Sir John A. Macdonald. I have read debates at the opening of a number of parliaments across the years and I find that on quite a number of occasions

there have been disputes. There have been occasions when some alternative person was proposed in opposition to the name suggested from the government side. True, in all the cases the choice of the government became the choice of the House of Commons. What interests me, however, is that gradually the house came to realize, although there might be differences over some things that were done in connection with the election of the speaker that basically he must be recognized not as the choice of the government nor as the choice of the prime minister but as the choice of the entire House of Commons.
The Right Hon. Arthur Meighen on March 8, 1922, speaking to a motion of the then prime minister, Mr. King, for the appointment of the speaker for that parliament, used the words I read a moment ago from Beau-chesne's third edition and then he went on to say:
Indeed, in the British parliament it has never been the practice even for a member of the government to move or second the selection of a speaker: that is left to the private members. In our parliament we have not in that special regard followed the British practice. No one would deny that a member acceptable to the administration should be selected; but I do deny the right of the administration-the right of the prime minister to announce to this house and to the country m advance whom we shall select as speaker.
In 1930 Mr. Bennett was prime minister and on September 8, when it was proposed that Mr. Black be appointed as speaker, Mr. King indicated he had no objection to the person of Mr. Black but he did object to the way in which Mr. Bennett had gone about announcing the appointment of Mr. Black, more or less installing him as speaker, even before his election had been accomplished by the House of Commons. In objecting to what was done at that time, Mr. King, as recorded at page 3 of Hansard for September 8, 1930, read some of the statements that Mr. Meighen had made in 1922 and put his stamp of approval on Mr. Meighen's statement:
. . . that the government have not any right as such to name a speaker, that the speaker is essentially an officer of the House of Commons: he '*S an appointee of the House of Commons and is in no sense an appointee of the government.
There, Mr. Speaker, you have both the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen and the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King making it extremely clear that the choice of the person to preside over the deliberations of this house is the prerogative of the House of Commons and not the prerogative of the government nor of the Prime Minister. It is clear that it took a few years to build up that tradition but it had certainly become firmly established by the twenties and thirties of this century.
House of Commons
In 1936 when Mr. King moved the nomination of a speaker for that parliament he ran into some difficulties because of certain things that had happened. He referred to the practice at Westminster of having a permanent speaker. I should like to interject that this matter seems to have been discussed a good many times in the history of the House of Commons and although it has been discussed at times when speakers were elected nothing seems to have been done about it in the meantime. At any rate, Mr. King on February 6, 1936, as reported at page 2 of Hansard for that date, said:
In Canada the practice since confederation has been different; the speaker has been nominated by a member of the ministry, the prime minister, in fact, and I think the nomination has in all cases been accepted by members of the commons. It is but right, that the ministry should have at least an opportunity to make known its view with regard to the person it thinks should be appointed to the high office of speaker.
I continue with these words used by Mr. King:
I wish to make it very clear, however, to hon. members, that the choice of a speaker is the choice of the commons itself, and that hon. members themselves must elect the one who is to be the occupant of that office.
Although on that occasion Mr. Bennett and Mr. Woodsworth had reason to object to some of the things the government was doing they both concurred in that statement made by Mr. King that the choosing of the speaker is the prerogative of the House of Commons and not the prerogative of the government nor of the prime minister.
Similarly on May 16, 1940, when Mr. King was moving the nomination of Mr. Glen he referred once more to the difference between the tradition at Westminster and the tradition here but as reported on page 2 of Hansard for that date he said this:
However, this difference is not in any way intended to imply any restriction of the freedom of members to make whatever choice they wish. The speaker of the house is not appointed by the government, he is elected by the commons. Members of the house are entirely free to make whatever choice they wish.
I said at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, that my grievance is against the Prime Minister. It is my considered view- and some of us have had time to think this over since the events of yesterday afternoon- that the Prime Minister has added insult to injury, that he has given this parliament a serious affront in what he did yesterday.

A week ago yesterday the Speaker of the House of Commons placed his

House of Commons
resignation before us. As found at page 5555 of Hansard for July 2, 1956, he put it in these words:
I place now my resignation before the house to take effect at the pleasure of the house. I would wish that it be accepted as soon as possible.
He then went on with further comments, which he began with the words, "This is my farewell speech."
In my view, Mr. Speaker did the right thing on that occasion; he did the honourable thing. He placed his resignation before the house. He made his own decision on the basis of what had transpired in days just previous to July 2; and not only did he do the right and honourable thing in offering his resignation, but speaking in parliamentary terms he did the correct thing in placing it in the hands of the House of Commons. It was there, Mr. Speaker, for the House of Commons to deal with. This is something that is one of the prerogatives of the House of Commons. The acting prime minister of that day, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), was quite correct, I think, in suggesting that this was a matter that might wait until the return of the Prime Minister yesterday; and so we waited with anticipation the return of the right hon. gentleman. Yesterday, with regard to the resignation offered the week before by the Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) chose to say that it was not really a resignation. I quote from page 5763 of Hansard of Monday, July 9. This is what the Prime Minister said:
Of course, all hon. members are aware that such a statement or declaration of intention does not constitute the formal action required as the actual resignation of a Speaker.
I do not think anyone will deny that, in the view of the Speaker, he was placing his resignation in the hands of the house for the house to deal with, when he took the course of action that he pursued on Monday, July 2. The Prime Minister took it upon himself to place on the Speaker's statement a different interpretation than that which the Speaker had placed upon it and a different interpretation than that which was understood by the house. Not only did the Prime Minister place this different interpretation upon the words of the Speaker. He violated the prerogatives that have been laid down over a number of decades by choosing to make by himself a decision as to who would be Speaker of the House of Commons for the balance of this parliament. I can imagine that some hon. members would like to argue with me and say that what we were confronted with at this stage is something different from that with which we are confronted at the beginning of a parliament

when we have no Speaker. Technically that statement is correct. Technically there has been no break in the Speakership in the House of Commons in this parliament. But in spirit, speaking virtually, from the time Mr. Speaker placed his resignation in the hands of the House of Commons on Monday July 2 until yesterday, we were really without a Speaker.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated earlier that the question of how the Speaker gets elected in this House of Commons has an extremely interesting history. There were earlier occasions when there were struggles and squabbles of one kind and another; but gradually it has been accepted that he is the choice of the whole House of Commons. Indeed it was in this very parliament, under the present Prime Minister, that I think we reached perhaps as high a point as we have ever reached when, at the opening of the first session of this parliament in 1953,- I think for the first time in history-the Prime Minister's motion that the present Speaker take the chair was seconded by the Leader of the Opposition. At the start of this parliament under the present Prime Minister we had reached a high point in the unanimity with which the house acts in the matter of electing a Speaker. Yesterday under the same Prime Minister we reached a low point, when the right of the House of Commons to have the say as to who is to be the presiding officer was taken away from the House of Commons-I do not think even the Liberal party had any say in it-and was exercised by the Prime Minister himself.
I have already said that I think His Honour the Speaker did the right and honourable thing on July 2, when he placed his resignation in the hands of this house. I am not now offering any words of criticism of the Speaker, despite what I might have felt about something that happened earlier this evening. I have refrained from any criticism on that score because I think a new issue has arisen, the issue of the rights of the House of Commons itself, rights which the Prime Minister himself has violated.
The reason I said earlier that I could have [DOT] related my remarks to the not too important issue raised by the hon. member for New Westminster was that I realized he was asking that parliament go home for the summer and I could have supported that suggestion because certainly I think it should

be going home right now, but not for the same reasons which he gave.
Because parliament has got into an atmosphere where we are not able to do the business of the country properly, it does not matter, from here on in this parliament, who is put in the chair, the present Speaker or someone else. If he is going to be chosen by the Prime Minister and given to the house on the Prime Minister's authority without any attempt to pay some regard to the decencies of parliamentary procedure that would simply continue to damage and destroy the atmosphere of this house.
I think most of us believe that certainly one of the most important institutions in Canada, if not the most important, is the parliament of Canada. The people of Canada have the right to have that institution on the highest possible level. The people of Canada have a right to have the discussions in this parliament take place on a basis of give-and-take, of argument and conflict, but nevertheless of understanding as to the points that we are discussing and with respect both ways and with respect for the Chair.
We have had an unfortunate atmosphere since the events of earlier this session, and I think it has become very clear that this parliament's prestige in the eyes of the Canadian people does not merit its being continued and that the Prime Minister, who will have the ultimate say as to when dissolution will take place, subject to the five-year limit, owes it to parliament and owes it to the people of Canada to give consideration to a very early dissolution of parliament and the calling of a general election.
I insist that the issue now-and I say this for the benefit of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration as well as others-is not with reference to things that have happened in the past and on which the house may have taken decisions. The issue that faces us in this house is pin-pointed by the dictatorial attitude of the Prime Minister yesterday in his disregard for the prerogatives of parliament. I feel more strongly now than I did when I urged on earlier occasions that there be a dissolution that that is the only course to follow. I hope that the Prime Minister will give serious consideration to this matter and do something about it at an early date.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the situation was such that I did not get the floor earlier so that there might be more time for this matter to be discussed, but even so I feel I should not speak longer, for I wish to leave at least the 12 minutes that there are tonight and the six minutes there are tomorrow for the Prime Minister to speak on this matter if he wishes to do so, and I trust he will.

But, if he does exercise that right, as I hope he will, I trust he will not say the kind of thing that will close the door to a proper consideration of what I think is now his duty to the Canadian people, namely, the early dissolution of parliament and the calling of a general election so that we might have a new parliament, clean and fresh, that can measure up to what the Canadian people have a right to expect.

There may come a time when he will not only have to think but be in a position to do what he thinks should be done; but that time has not yet arrived.
With respect to everything the hon. gentleman has said about the choice of the Speaker, I am in full agreement, and it did not require 89 years of practice to make it absolutely crystal clear that the Speaker was the choice of the House of Commons. However, the hon. gentleman, who referred to sections 44 and 45 of the British North America Act, certainly overlooked, and many others in the house have overlooked, the provision of section 49 of the British North America Act, which provides that the actions of the House of Commons do not have to be by the unanimous decision of the House of Commons but that they are the result of decisions by the majority of the members of the House of Commons.
It has been sought to be established for quite a long time in this House of Commons that it was not the supporters of the government who had the right to make decisions but that it was the members of the opposition, and that whenever there was any suggestion put before the house with which the members of the opposition did not agree it was wrong, unconstitutional and a contempt of parliament not to take into account their views instead of taking into account the views of the majority sent here by the Canadian people-

-to make the decisions that are required to be made to carry on the business of the country. It is not by any accident that the party of which I have the honour to be the leader at the present time has been in office now for 21 years and plans to continue in office for several years longer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Now, with respect to what I did yesterday, the hon. gentleman says that that is an act of contempt of parliament. I submit that it was an act of full respect for the rights and privileges of parliament.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has been posing, and with some justification, as an expert on the rules and precedents of parliamentary institutions. The hon. gentleman knows as well as I do that there has never been any formal acceptance by the House of Commons here or by the House of Commons in the United Kingdom of the resignation of a Speaker. A Speaker who chooses to resign does resign and it is the act of his own will that creates the vacancy required under the British North America Act to make way for the appointment of a new Speaker. The hon. gentleman knows as well as I do, and as well as all other hon. members who have not made as profound a study as he has of the rules and precedents, that what was stated by Mr. Speaker on Monday, the 2nd of July, did not vacate his office and that it was expected there would be some other formal action that would bring about the situation provided for in section 45 of the British North America Act, that is to say, a vacancy happening in the office by resignation or otherwise.
That being the situation, I felt that it was necessary for me to say to the house whether or not I was going to take any formal action to bring about a vacancy in the office of Speaker. What I did yesterday was to declare to the house that, having ascertained that the Speaker was willing to have his duty to parliament and to the country regarded as higher than his natural desire to be able to meet the criticisms that had been and were still being levelled against him, I felt under no obligation to take any action in respect of the statements that had been made on the 2nd of July.
I appointed no Speaker. I made no pretence of appointing any Speaker. I proposed the motion, which was seconded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), made at the beginning of this parliament that the present Speaker take the chair for this parliament. I did that because I realized, as the hon. member realizes, that it is desirable to have the appointment of the Speaker in the form in which it is made represent what is provided for by the constitution, that is to say, an appointment by the House of Commons and not an appointment by the government.

House of Commons
I remember that both in 1949 and in 1953 newspapermen were anxious to find out whom I was going to propose for the speakership. I told them that the speakership was something that was within the jurisdiction of the House of Commons itself and that I could give them no information, that I had in mind the gentleman I wished to suggest to the house to appoint but that he would become Speaker only if and when he had become appointed by the House of Commons. He is still Speaker of the House of Commons because there has never been the formal act required by the constitution to create a vacancy in his office, and I felt that it was desirable as soon as possible after my return to state publicly that I was not going to take any action to bring about a vacancy unless Mr. Speaker himself refused to continue to carry out the responsibilities of the office which he has discharged with knowledge, competence and distinction.
Whatever the hon. gentleman may think of my conduct, and I know that he is sincere, I do not think that my conduct requires me to advise His Excellency to dissolve parliament at this time. The hon. gentleman has said that is the only matter with which he is dealing as his grievance at this moment. Well, I am not going to satisfy that grievance and his grievance must persist if the only way in which it caj be removed is by my stating here that I have come to the conclusion that I have acted in a way that makes it improper for me to continue to be a member of parliament. I do not agree that that is the case, and I am convinced, as I was convinced yesterday, that in informing the house that Mr. Speaker was willing to continue I was informing a majority, a large and overwhelming majority made up not only of those who support this government, of something which was very agreeable to them.
If the hon. gentleman feels that I mistook the sense and feeling of the majority in this house he knows that he can at any time put on the order paper a notice of motion to remove the Speaker from the chair and he will see-

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON OVERTIME AND WAGE RATES ON FEDERAL WORKS AT LA SCIE
speechtext:
On June 19 the hon. member for Comox-Alberni asked me several questions referring to overtime and wage rates on federal works at La Scie, Newfoundland. At that time I stated that our Newfoundland officer had been instructed to investigate the complaint and make a report.
The first complaint was that the companies concerned were working their employees in excess of the authorized hours. The second complaint was that they were paying local workers less than mainland workers for the same work; and third, our representative was asked to investigate and determine whether the companies should be required to pay
penalty overtime rates for hours worked in excess of the statutory hours.
Our officer has now reported in the negative on the first two complaints, and on the third that he was making an effort to effect an understanding with the company on the question of overtime payments.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. I note in this morning's press that Vice President Nixon of the United States has issued a warning to the neutral free countries of the world against accepting any economic or military aid from Russia. Does the Prime Minister consider the time has come for a warning from this government to those countries which are being offered Russian aid; that is, a warning as to the dangers of accepting these offers?
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I would hesitate to suggest that the Canadian government issue any warning against the acceptance of aid by less developed countries though, of course, there may be some dangers involved in doing so. But I think the fact that there would be assistance to underdeveloped countries is a meritorious fact in itself. I do not think we would put ourselves in the position where we

Inquiries of the Ministry might appear to be saying you should get the aid and if you refuse to take it from the countries behind the iron curtain we shall see that you get it from other sources. We are not in a position to do that. There has been a lot of propaganda about proffered aid, and I think it has gone beyond the actual benefits that those who seem to have been offered aid would receive from such offers.
It is very difficult to attempt to intervene in the domestic affairs of other countries. Of course a country like the United States may be in a position to say, "If you do not take aid from Russia we shall see that you get it from us", but we are not in a position to make any such broad statement.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned last night at ten o'clock I was trying to show the relation between these Yankee dollars and Canadian jobs. I am not going to keep the house too long today, because I do not want to hold up this session too long; I am very anxious to get back to Vancouver. I am particularly anxious to get back to Vancouver because since I finished the first half of my speech last night and today when I am beginning the second half, I have had news of my second new granddaughter since Easter. I would remind hon. gentlemen of the good old British Columbia custom that whereas fathers must give out cigars when sons or daughters appear, grandfathers always receive cigars from all quarters of the house.
I want to refer particularly to one section of the speech of the Leader of the Opposition when, as reported at page 5780 of Hansard, he said:
We all share the satisfaction in the growth and development that has already taken place. But this is only a promise of what can happen. Government policies should encourage the development of our own resources, should promote the processing of those resources in Canada, should correct our unfavourable trade balance, should assure the participation by Canadians in the development and processing of our resources, and should assure

Natural Resources-Development opportunity and employment for all Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific wherever they may live.
As I listened to the hon. members of the Conservative opposition yesterday developing their case, it seemed to me that I heard echoes of old, unhappy, far-off things and battles of long ago, because there was the distinct echo of 1911 in this approach. I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that there would be now anything as blatant as the slogan which won the election of 1911, namely "No truck nor trade with the Yankees". However, I am submitting that the Conservative opposition are on a slippery slope now, and that they could easily continue down the decline until they got themselves in a position even more dangerous for this country than that of advocating "No truck nor trade with the Yankees" as they did so successfully in 1911.
What I want to show, Mr. Speaker, is that there is a very real connection between these Yankee dollars which some of my hon. friends in the Conservative opposition would keep away from Canada, and Canadian jobs. I do not know whether they would chase out the dollars which are already invested here in the factories, in the pipe lines and in all the other things that go to make up the prosperity of Canada, or whether they would confine themselves to keeping out new investments in Canada; but I want to submit that Yankee dollars invested in Canada mean good jobs for the Canadian people. God help this country if we are ever foolish enough to turn away those Yankee dollars simply to make a convenient election slogan for a desperate party, or for politicians who have not thought things through.
Last night I referred to a very admirable volume, "Canada's International Investment Position, 1926-1954", and I submitted that it is a bargain at $1 from the queen's printer. On page 44 of that volume we get an exact breakdown of all the different industries in Canada, exactly what percentages United States-owned companies obtain in the Canadian market and exactly what percentage of employment is given to Canadians by that United States investment. Working from the bottom upward, 1 shall read the statistics on page 44:
