speechtext: Is not the hon. member out of order?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: I am prepared to answer that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: The hon. gentleman poses as a great expert on the rules. I am asking if that question has not been settled by vote of the house and therefore should not be raised again. I should like him to give an answer to that question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: I am quite prepared to answer that question. In fact, I would be happy to listen to a speech by the minister on that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: I think it would be out of order to make a speech.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Oh, shut up.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: I may tell the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) that one of the reasons I am talking about the present situation is precisely because I realized that a point of order could be raised if I talked about things that happened prior to the time that certain votes were taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
That is not answering my question.
House of Commons

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: There was a vote on the question as to whether or not the Speaker should be censured.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: No. That is not the question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: There was also a vote, on party lines, on the motion of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) calling for dissolution of this house and an election.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: And that question was decided.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: But, Mr. Speaker, what I am talking about has happened since then. I base my contention that the time has come for dissolution not just on the things that took place in days gone by and on which there may have been decisions by the majority of this house, even though in some of those cases the decision was really not valid unless it was unanimous. I base my protest on what happened yesterday afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: In other words, the hon. gentleman is objecting to a decision of the house.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Sit down.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: I am asking if the hon. gentleman is not setting himself up above the house. A decision was made by the house by an overwhelming majority. He is now asking that that decision should be reversed.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: The hon. member will have the opportunity to make a speech.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: The house decided on Tuesday, June 26, by a majority vote that there should not be a dissolution. To the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration does that mean that there is never to be a dissolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
Does it mean that this
government is to stay in office forever? Would that vote of the house deny to the members of the government the right to meet at any time and decide on dissolution when they wished to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
Not at all; but if I may
answer the question which the hon. gentleman asked, I will do so. What it means is that no hon. member has a right in this session in debate to raise the same question again for decision by the house.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
That is the rule and the hon. gentleman knows it very well.

House of Commons

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: The decision, even though it was only a majority decision, was on the motion of the Leader of the Opposition calling for dissolution not in the abstract but on the basis of what had happened prior to the time he made that motion. I call for dissolution of this parliament, if for no other reason, on the basis of what happened yesterday. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration cannot get around the fact that something new in terms of damaging parliament has been added to the picture by the action of the Prime Minister yesterday.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: A very flimsy basis.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated earlier that the question of how the Speaker gets elected in this House of Commons has an extremely interesting history. There were earlier occasions when there were struggles and squabbles of one kind and another; but gradually it has been accepted that he is the choice of the whole House of Commons. Indeed it was in this very parliament, under the present Prime Minister, that I think we reached perhaps as high a point as we have ever reached when, at the opening of the first session of this parliament in 1953,- I think for the first time in history-the Prime Minister's motion that the present Speaker take the chair was seconded by the Leader of the Opposition. At the start of this parliament under the present Prime Minister we had reached a high point in the unanimity with which the house acts in the matter of electing a Speaker. Yesterday under the same Prime Minister we reached a low point, when the right of the House of Commons to have the say as to who is to be the presiding officer was taken away from the House of Commons-I do not think even the Liberal party had any say in it-and was exercised by the Prime Minister himself.
I have already said that I think His Honour the Speaker did the right and honourable thing on July 2, when he placed his resignation in the hands of this house. I am not now offering any words of criticism of the Speaker, despite what I might have felt about something that happened earlier this evening. I have refrained from any criticism on that score because I think a new issue has arisen, the issue of the rights of the House of Commons itself, rights which the Prime Minister himself has violated.
The reason I said earlier that I could have [DOT] related my remarks to the not too important issue raised by the hon. member for New Westminster was that I realized he was asking that parliament go home for the summer and I could have supported that suggestion because certainly I think it should

be going home right now, but not for the same reasons which he gave.
Because parliament has got into an atmosphere where we are not able to do the business of the country properly, it does not matter, from here on in this parliament, who is put in the chair, the present Speaker or someone else. If he is going to be chosen by the Prime Minister and given to the house on the Prime Minister's authority without any attempt to pay some regard to the decencies of parliamentary procedure that would simply continue to damage and destroy the atmosphere of this house.
I think most of us believe that certainly one of the most important institutions in Canada, if not the most important, is the parliament of Canada. The people of Canada have the right to have that institution on the highest possible level. The people of Canada have a right to have the discussions in this parliament take place on a basis of give-and-take, of argument and conflict, but nevertheless of understanding as to the points that we are discussing and with respect both ways and with respect for the Chair.
We have had an unfortunate atmosphere since the events of earlier this session, and I think it has become very clear that this parliament's prestige in the eyes of the Canadian people does not merit its being continued and that the Prime Minister, who will have the ultimate say as to when dissolution will take place, subject to the five-year limit, owes it to parliament and owes it to the people of Canada to give consideration to a very early dissolution of parliament and the calling of a general election.
I insist that the issue now-and I say this for the benefit of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration as well as others-is not with reference to things that have happened in the past and on which the house may have taken decisions. The issue that faces us in this house is pin-pointed by the dictatorial attitude of the Prime Minister yesterday in his disregard for the prerogatives of parliament. I feel more strongly now than I did when I urged on earlier occasions that there be a dissolution that that is the only course to follow. I hope that the Prime Minister will give serious consideration to this matter and do something about it at an early date.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the situation was such that I did not get the floor earlier so that there might be more time for this matter to be discussed, but even so I feel I should not speak longer, for I wish to leave at least the 12 minutes that there are tonight and the six minutes there are tomorrow for the Prime Minister to speak on this matter if he wishes to do so, and I trust he will.

But, if he does exercise that right, as I hope he will, I trust he will not say the kind of thing that will close the door to a proper consideration of what I think is now his duty to the Canadian people, namely, the early dissolution of parliament and the calling of a general election so that we might have a new parliament, clean and fresh, that can measure up to what the Canadian people have a right to expect.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think that I shall require even the 12 minutes that remained a moment ago, when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre sat down, and the six minutes of tomorrow to tell him that it is not what he thinks I should do that is going to be done. There may come a time when he will not only have to think but be in a position to do what he thinks should be done; but that time has not yet arrived.
With respect to everything the hon. gentleman has said about the choice of the Speaker, I am in full agreement, and it did not require 89 years of practice to make it absolutely crystal clear that the Speaker was the choice of the House of Commons. However, the hon. gentleman, who referred to sections 44 and 45 of the British North America Act, certainly overlooked, and many others in the house have overlooked, the provision of section 49 of the British North America Act, which provides that the actions of the House of Commons do not have to be by the unanimous decision of the House of Commons but that they are the result of decisions by the majority of the members of the House of Commons.
It has been sought to be established for quite a long time in this House of Commons that it was not the supporters of the government who had the right to make decisions but that it was the members of the opposition, and that whenever there was any suggestion put before the house with which the members of the opposition did not agree it was wrong, unconstitutional and a contempt of parliament not to take into account their views instead of taking into account the views of the majority sent here by the Canadian people-

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
-to make the decisions that are required to be made to carry on the business of the country. It is not by any accident that the party of which I have the honour to be the leader at the present time has been in office now for 21 years and plans to continue in office for several years longer.
House of Commons

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: 1957 will be the end.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Now, with respect to what I did yesterday, the hon. gentleman says that that is an act of contempt of parliament. I submit that it was an act of full respect for the rights and privileges of parliament.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has been posing, and with some justification, as an expert on the rules and precedents of parliamentary institutions. The hon. gentleman knows as well as I do that there has never been any formal acceptance by the House of Commons here or by the House of Commons in the United Kingdom of the resignation of a Speaker. A Speaker who chooses to resign does resign and it is the act of his own will that creates the vacancy required under the British North America Act to make way for the appointment of a new Speaker. The hon. gentleman knows as well as I do, and as well as all other hon. members who have not made as profound a study as he has of the rules and precedents, that what was stated by Mr. Speaker on Monday, the 2nd of July, did not vacate his office and that it was expected there would be some other formal action that would bring about the situation provided for in section 45 of the British North America Act, that is to say, a vacancy happening in the office by resignation or otherwise.
That being the situation, I felt that it was necessary for me to say to the house whether or not I was going to take any formal action to bring about a vacancy in the office of Speaker. What I did yesterday was to declare to the house that, having ascertained that the Speaker was willing to have his duty to parliament and to the country regarded as higher than his natural desire to be able to meet the criticisms that had been and were still being levelled against him, I felt under no obligation to take any action in respect of the statements that had been made on the 2nd of July.
I appointed no Speaker. I made no pretence of appointing any Speaker. I proposed the motion, which was seconded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), made at the beginning of this parliament that the present Speaker take the chair for this parliament. I did that because I realized, as the hon. member realizes, that it is desirable to have the appointment of the Speaker in the form in which it is made represent what is provided for by the constitution, that is to say, an appointment by the House of Commons and not an appointment by the government.

House of Commons
I remember that both in 1949 and in 1953 newspapermen were anxious to find out whom I was going to propose for the speakership. I told them that the speakership was something that was within the jurisdiction of the House of Commons itself and that I could give them no information, that I had in mind the gentleman I wished to suggest to the house to appoint but that he would become Speaker only if and when he had become appointed by the House of Commons. He is still Speaker of the House of Commons because there has never been the formal act required by the constitution to create a vacancy in his office, and I felt that it was desirable as soon as possible after my return to state publicly that I was not going to take any action to bring about a vacancy unless Mr. Speaker himself refused to continue to carry out the responsibilities of the office which he has discharged with knowledge, competence and distinction.
Whatever the hon. gentleman may think of my conduct, and I know that he is sincere, I do not think that my conduct requires me to advise His Excellency to dissolve parliament at this time. The hon. gentleman has said that is the only matter with which he is dealing as his grievance at this moment. Well, I am not going to satisfy that grievance and his grievance must persist if the only way in which it caj be removed is by my stating here that I have come to the conclusion that I have acted in a way that makes it improper for me to continue to be a member of parliament. I do not agree that that is the case, and I am convinced, as I was convinced yesterday, that in informing the house that Mr. Speaker was willing to continue I was informing a majority, a large and overwhelming majority made up not only of those who support this government, of something which was very agreeable to them.
If the hon. gentleman feels that I mistook the sense and feeling of the majority in this house he knows that he can at any time put on the order paper a notice of motion to remove the Speaker from the chair and he will see-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: On a question of privilege-

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Sit down.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: On a question of privilege, will the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) not admit that I made it clear that I did not think it mattered who is in the chair. Will the Prime Minister-

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Sit down.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: -not agree that I made it clear that it was not the resignation of the Speaker I was suggesting but rather the dissolution of parliament?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: I know that it was the dissolution of parliament that the hon. gentleman was suggesting, but he was suggesting the dissolution of parliament because I had stated yesterday that I believed that it was the will of the majority in this house, if Mr. Speaker was willing to do so, that he continue to preside over our deliberations. That being the only reason urged by my hon. friend for a dissolution of parliament, I consider it to be a very insufficient reason.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: You will not need any more votes, just your opinion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman thinks that I am mistaken about how the votes would go in this house he knows how he can test that opinion.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: You are sure they will all vote for you.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is ten o'clock. I will not continue now unless it should be the unanimous feeling of the house that the six minutes additional should be taken up tonight.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
Ten o'clock. You have said
too much now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext: You cannot take it any more.

maintopic: ACTION OF PRIME MINISTER WITH RESPECT TO THE OFFICE OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
Sit down and take it.
